title: Chapter 11
paragraphs: Once they were inside the studio, Mihailov took another look at his visitors and made a note of Vronsky's expression too — particularly his jaws. Although his artist's eye was working ceaselessly, gathering material, and although he felt a steadily mounting agitation as the moment of having his work judged drew closer, he rapidly and subtly built up, out of imperceptible signs, a mental image of these three people.

That fellow (Golenishtchev) was a Russian living here. Mihailov could not remember his surname, or where he had met him, or what they had talked about. He only remembered his face, as he remembered every face he had ever seen; but he also remembered that this was one of the faces filed away in his memory in the huge category of the falsely consequential and poor in expression. The thick hair and very high forehead lent the face an air of consequence, while it had only one real expression — a petty, childish, peevish look concentrated just above the bridge of the narrow nose. Vronsky and Madame Karenina, Mihailov supposed, must be distinguished, wealthy Russians who knew nothing about art, like all such wealthy Russians, but were posing as amateurs and connoisseurs. "Most likely they've already looked through all the antiquities, and now they're making the rounds of the studios of the new painters — the German humbug, and the crackpot Pre-Raphaelite English fellow — and have only come to me to round out the survey," he thought. He was well acquainted with the way dilettanti have (and the cleverer they were, the worse he found them) of looking at the work of contemporary artists with the sole aim of being able to say that art is a thing of the past — that the more one sees of the new men, the clearer it becomes how inimitable the works of the great old masters have remained. He expected all of this; he saw it all in their faces; he saw it in the careless indifference with which they talked among themselves, stared at the lay figures and busts, and strolled about at their leisure, waiting for him to uncover his picture. But despite all this, while he was turning over his studies, pulling up the blinds, and taking off the sheet, he was in a state of intense excitement, especially since, in spite of his conviction that all distinguished, wealthy Russians were bound to be brutes and fools, he liked Vronsky, and still more Anna.

"Here, if you please," he said, stepping aside with his quick gait and pointing to his picture. "It's the exhortation to Pilate. Matthew, chapter xxvii," he said, feeling his lips beginning to tremble with emotion. He moved away and stood behind them.

For the few seconds the visitors were gazing at the picture in silence, Mihailov too gazed at it, with the indifferent eye of an outsider. For those few seconds he was sure in advance that a higher, more just judgment would come from them — from the very visitors he had been despising a moment earlier. He forgot everything he had thought about his picture during the three years he had been painting it; he forgot all the qualities of it that had been absolutely certain to him — he saw the picture through their indifferent, new, outsider's eyes, and saw nothing good in it. He saw in the foreground Pilate's irritated face and the serene face of Christ, and in the background the figures of Pilate's retinue and the face of John watching what was happening. Every face that, with such agony, such blunders and corrections, had grown up inside him with its own particular character, every face that had given him such torments and such raptures, all those faces transposed so many times for the sake of the harmony of the whole, all the shades of color and tone he had reached only after such labor — all of it together now seemed to him, looking through their eyes, the merest vulgarity, something that had been done a thousand times before. The face dearest to him, the face of Christ, the center of the picture, which had given him such ecstasy as it had unfolded for him, was utterly lost to him when he looked at the picture with their eyes. He saw a well-painted (no, not even that — he distinctly saw now a mass of defects) repetition of those endless Christs by Titian, Raphael, Rubens, and the same soldiers and Pilate. It was all commonplace, poor, and stale, and positively badly painted — weak and uneven. They would be quite right to keep up hypocritically polite phrases in the painter's presence and to pity him and laugh at him once they were alone again.
The silence (though it lasted no more than a minute) became unbearable to him. To break it, and to show he was not agitated, he made an effort and turned to Golenishtchev.
"I think I've had the pleasure of meeting you before," he said, glancing uneasily first at Anna, then at Vronsky, afraid of missing the slightest shade of their expression.

"To be sure! We met at Rossi's — do you remember, at that _soirée_ where that Italian lady recited, the new Rachel?" Golenishtchev answered easily, taking his eyes off the picture without the slightest regret and turning to the artist.
Noticing, however, that Mihailov was expecting some criticism of the picture, he said:

"Your picture has come on a great deal since I saw it last; and what strikes me particularly now, as it did then, is the figure of Pilate. You really know the man — a good-natured, capable fellow, but an official through and through, who doesn't know what it is he is doing. But I rather think...."

Mihailov's whole mobile face lit up at once; his eyes sparkled. He tried to say something but could not get a word out for emotion, and pretended to be coughing. Low as his opinion of Golenishtchev's capacity for understanding art was, trifling as the true observation about the accuracy of Pilate's expression as an official was, and offensive as it might have seemed for so unimportant a remark to be made while nothing was said about the more serious points, Mihailov was in an ecstasy of delight at this remark. He had himself thought about Pilate's figure exactly what Golenishtchev said. That this reflection was just one of millions of reflections that, as Mihailov knew for certain, would all be true, did not diminish for him the significance of Golenishtchev's remark. His heart warmed to Golenishtchev for it, and from a state of depression he suddenly passed to ecstasy. At once the whole of his picture came alive for him, in all the indescribable complexity of every living thing. Mihailov tried again to say that this was just how he understood Pilate, but his lips would not stop quivering, and he could not get the words out. Vronsky and Anna too said something in that lowered tone in which, partly to spare the artist's feelings and partly to avoid saying out loud something silly — so easily said when talking of art — people usually speak at exhibitions of pictures. Mihailov imagined that the picture had made an impression on them too. He went up to them.

"How marvelous Christ's expression is!" said Anna. Of everything she saw, she liked that expression best, and she felt that it was the center of the picture, and so praise of it would please the artist. "One can see that He is pitying Pilate."

This too was one of the million true reflections that could be found in his picture, and in the figure of Christ. She had said He was pitying Pilate. There ought indeed to be an expression of pity in Christ's expression, since there is an expression of love, of heavenly peace, of readiness for death, and of a sense of the futility of words. Of course there is the look of an official in Pilate and of pity in Christ, since one is the embodiment of fleshly life and the other of spiritual life. All this and a great deal more flashed through Mihailov's mind.

"Yes, and how that figure is done — what atmosphere! One could walk all the way round it," said Golenishtchev, unmistakably showing by his remark that he did not approve of the meaning and idea of the figure.

"Yes, there's wonderful mastery!" said Vronsky. "How those figures in the background stand out! There you have technique," he said, addressing Golenishtchev, alluding to a conversation between them about Vronsky's despair of attaining this kind of technique.

"Yes, yes, marvelous!" Golenishtchev and Anna agreed. Despite his excited state, the sentence about technique sent a pang through Mihailov's heart, and looking angrily at Vronsky he suddenly scowled. He had often heard this word technique, and was utterly unable to understand what was meant by it. He knew that by that term people meant a mechanical facility for painting or drawing, entirely separate from its subject. He had often noticed that even in actual praise technique was set against essential quality, as though one could paint well something that was bad. He knew that a great deal of attention and care was needed in stripping away the coverings so as not to damage the creation itself, and to strip them all away; but there was no art of painting in that — no technique of any sort. If what he saw could be revealed to a little child or to his cook, the child or the cook would be able to peel the wrappings off what was seen. And the most experienced and adroit painter could not by mere mechanical facility paint anything if the lines of the subject were not first revealed to him. Besides, he saw that if it came to talking about technique, he could not be praised for it. In everything he had painted and repainted, he saw faults that hurt his eyes, coming from carelessness in stripping off the wrappings — faults he could not now correct without ruining the whole. And in nearly all the figures and faces, too, he saw remnants of wrappings not perfectly removed that spoiled the picture.
"One thing might be said, if you'll allow me the remark...." Golenishtchev observed.
"Oh, I'd be delighted, please," said Mihailov with a forced smile.
"That is, that you make Him the man-god, and not the God-man. But I know that was what you meant to do."
"I cannot paint a Christ that is not in my heart," Mihailov said gloomily.

"Yes; but in that case, if you'll allow me to say what I think.... Your picture is so fine that my comment cannot detract from it, and besides, it is only my personal opinion. With you it is different. Your very motive is different. But take Ivanov. I think that if Christ is brought down to the level of a historical figure, it would have been better for Ivanov to pick some other historical subject — fresh, untouched."
"But what if this is the greatest subject offered to art?"

"If one looked, one would find others. But the point is that art cannot endure doubt and discussion. And in front of Ivanov's picture, the question arises for the believer and the unbeliever alike — 'Is it God, or is it not God?' — and the unity of the impression is destroyed."
"Why so? I should think that for educated people," said Mihailov, "the question cannot exist."
Golenishtchev did not agree with this, and confounded Mihailov by sticking to his first idea that unity of impression is essential to art.
Mihailov was greatly disturbed, but could find nothing to say in defense of his own idea.

title: Chapter 12
paragraphs: Anna and Vronsky had been exchanging glances for some time, sorry that their friend was still riding his wave of cleverness. At last Vronsky, without waiting for the artist, drifted off to another small picture.
"Oh, how exquisite! What a lovely thing! A gem! How exquisite!" they cried in one voice.

"What is it that pleases them so much?" Mihailov wondered. He had genuinely forgotten this picture he had painted three years ago. He had forgotten all the agonies and the elations he had lived through with it, back when, for months on end, it had been the single thought that haunted him day and night. He had forgotten it, as he always forgot pictures once they were finished. He did not even like looking at it, and had only dragged it out because he was expecting an Englishman who wanted to buy it.
"Oh, that's only an old study," he said.
"How fine it is!" said Golenishtchev, also clearly sincere, falling under the picture's spell himself.

Two boys were fishing in the shade of a willow tree. The older one had just dropped his hook in and was carefully drawing the float out from behind a bush, entirely absorbed in what he was doing. The other, a little younger, lay in the grass leaning on his elbows, his tangled, flaxen head propped in his hands, staring at the water with his dreamy blue eyes. What was he thinking about?

The enthusiasm over this picture stirred some of the old feeling for it in Mihailov, but he feared and disliked this squandering of emotion on things already finished, and so, even though the praise was sweet to him, he tried to draw his visitors away to a third picture.
But Vronsky asked whether the picture was for sale. To Mihailov at that moment, keyed up by the visit, it was extremely distasteful to talk about money.
"It is hung there to be sold," he answered, scowling darkly.

Once the visitors had gone, Mihailov sat down opposite the picture of Pilate and Christ and turned over in his mind what had been said, and what, though unspoken, had been implied. Strangely enough, what had carried such weight while they were there, while he had mentally put himself in their place, suddenly lost all importance for him. He began to look at his picture again with his own complete artist's eye, and was soon back in that mood of conviction about the picture's potential perfection — and therefore its significance — a conviction essential to the most intense fervor, shutting out every other interest, the only state in which he could work at all.

Christ's foreshortened leg, though — that wasn't right. He picked up his palette and set to work. As he corrected the leg he kept glancing at the figure of John in the background, which his visitors had not even noticed, but which he knew was beyond perfection. When he had finished the leg he wanted to touch up that figure too, but he felt too stirred up for it. He could not work when he was cold, and he could not work when he was too moved and saw everything too vividly. There was only one stage in the transition from coldness to inspiration where work was actually possible. Today he was too agitated. He started to cover the picture, but he stopped, holding the cloth in his hand, and, smiling blissfully, stared a long time at the figure of John. At last, as if tearing himself away with regret, he dropped the cloth and, exhausted but happy, went home.

Vronsky, Anna, and Golenishtchev, on their way home, were unusually lively and cheerful. They talked about Mihailov and his pictures. The word _talent_ — by which they meant an inborn, almost physical aptitude apart from brain and heart, an expression they reached for to cover everything the artist had drawn from life — kept turning up in their conversation, as though they needed to sum up something they had no real grasp of but still wanted to discuss. They agreed there was no denying his talent, but his talent could not develop for lack of education — the standard defect, as they put it, of our Russian artists. But the picture of the boys had stamped itself on their memories, and they kept circling back to it. "What an exquisite thing! How well he has pulled it off, and how simply! He doesn't even realize how good it is. Yes, I mustn't let it slip; I must buy it," said Vronsky.

title: Chapter 13
paragraphs: Mihailov sold Vronsky his picture, and agreed to paint a portrait of Anna. On the day fixed, he showed up and started the work.

From the fifth sitting on, the portrait struck everyone, especially Vronsky, not just by the likeness but by the way it captured her particular beauty. It was strange how Mihailov had managed to discover precisely that beauty of hers. "You'd have to know and love her the way I have loved her to find the sweetest expression of her soul," Vronsky thought — even though it was only from this portrait that he himself had learned what that sweetest expression looked like. But the expression rang so true that he, and other people too, felt as if they had known it for years.
"I've been struggling along forever and getting nowhere," he said about his own portrait of her, "and he just looked at her and painted it. That's what technique is."

"That will come," Golenishtchev assured him soothingly. In Golenishtchev's view, Vronsky had both talent and — more importantly — culture, which gave him a broader outlook on art. Golenishtchev's faith in Vronsky's talent was propped up by his own need for Vronsky's sympathy and approval of his articles and ideas, and he felt the praise and support had to flow both ways.

In another man's house, and especially in Vronsky's palazzo, Mihailov was a completely different man from the one in his studio. He behaved with a stiff, hostile politeness, as though afraid of getting closer to people he did not respect. He called Vronsky "your excellency," and despite Anna's and Vronsky's invitations he would never stay for dinner, and would not show up except for the sittings. Anna treated him even more warmly than she treated other people and was very grateful for her portrait. Vronsky was more than cordial with him, and was plainly curious to hear the artist's opinion of his own picture. Golenishtchev never missed an opportunity to drip sound ideas about art into Mihailov. But Mihailov stayed equally cold toward all of them. Anna could tell from his eyes that he liked looking at her, but he avoided talking to her. When Vronsky talked about his painting, Mihailov met it with stubborn silence, and he was just as stubbornly silent when shown Vronsky's picture. He was unmistakably bored by Golenishtchev's conversation and didn't bother to argue with him.

On the whole Mihailov, with his reserved, off-putting, almost hostile manner, came to be disliked by them the more they got to know him; and they were glad when the sittings were finished and they were left in possession of a magnificent portrait and he stopped coming. Golenishtchev was the first to put into words an idea that had occurred to all of them — that Mihailov was simply jealous of Vronsky.

"Not envious, let's say, since he has _talent_; but it galls him that a wealthy man at the top of society — a count, no less (you know how they all loathe a title) — can without any particular effort do as well, if not better, than someone who has given his entire life to it. And above all it's a question of culture, which he lacks."
Vronsky defended Mihailov, but deep down he believed it, because in his view a man from a different, lower world was bound to be envious.

Anna's portrait — the same subject painted from life by him and by Mihailov — should have shown Vronsky the gap between them; but he didn't see it. Only after Mihailov's portrait was finished did he give up working on his own portrait of Anna, deciding now that it wasn't needed. He carried on with his picture of medieval life. He himself, and Golenishtchev, and Anna even more, thought it was very good, because it resembled the famous pictures they knew far more than Mihailov's picture did.

Mihailov, meanwhile, although Anna's portrait fascinated him deeply, was even more relieved than they were when the sittings ended and he no longer had to sit through Golenishtchev's lectures on art and could forget about Vronsky's painting. He knew there was no stopping Vronsky from amusing himself with painting; he knew Vronsky and every other dilettante had a perfect right to paint whatever they liked, but he found it distasteful. You couldn't stop a man from making himself a big wax doll and kissing it. But if the man were to bring the doll over and sit down across from someone in love and start caressing his doll the way the lover caressed the woman he loved, it would disgust the lover. That was exactly the kind of disgust Mihailov felt at the sight of Vronsky's painting: he found it both ridiculous and infuriating, both pitiful and offensive.

Vronsky's interest in painting and the Middle Ages did not last. He had enough taste for painting to be unable to finish his picture. The picture stalled. He was dimly aware that its defects, barely visible at first, would become glaring if he kept at it. He was in the same fix as Golenishtchev, who felt that he had nothing to say and kept fooling himself with the theory that his idea was not yet ripe, that he was still working it out and gathering materials. That self-deception drove Golenishtchev to bitterness and torment, but Vronsky was incapable of fooling and tormenting himself, and even less capable of bitterness. With his usual decisiveness, with no explanation and no apology, he simply stopped painting.

But without that occupation, the life of Vronsky and Anna — who was puzzled by his loss of interest — struck them as unbearably dull in an Italian town. The palazzo suddenly seemed glaringly old and dirty, the stains on the curtains, the cracks in the floors, the chipped plaster on the cornices became so unpleasantly conspicuous, and the unchanging sameness of Golenishtchev, the Italian professor, and the German traveler became so tiring, that something had to change. They decided to go to Russia, to the country. In Petersburg Vronsky planned to settle a division of the land with his brother, while Anna meant to see her son. The summer they intended to spend on Vronsky's large family estate.

title: Chapter 14
paragraphs: Levin had been married three months. He was happy, but not at all in the way he had expected to be. At every turn he found his old dreams disappointed and new, unexpected surprises of happiness. He was happy; but on stepping into family life he saw at every turn that it was utterly different from what he had imagined. At every step he felt what a man would feel who, after admiring the smooth, happy glide of a little boat on a lake, climbs into that little boat himself. He found that it wasn't only a matter of sitting still and drifting smoothly; that he also had to think, and not forget for a moment where he was going; that there was water under him, and that he had to row; that his unaccustomed hands would blister; and that it was only watching it that was easy — actually doing it, however delightful, was very hard.

As a bachelor, when he had watched other people's married life, taken in the petty annoyances, the squabbles, the jealousy, he had only smiled contemptuously to himself. In his own future married life there could be, he was convinced, nothing of that kind; even the outward forms, he had assumed, would be utterly unlike everyone else's in every respect. And then all at once, instead of his life with his wife being shaped on its own private pattern, it turned out to be made up precisely of the petty details he had despised before, but which now, without his choosing it, had taken on an extraordinary importance that there was no use fighting. And Levin saw that organizing all these details was not at all as easy as he had imagined. Although Levin believed he had the most precise notions of domestic life, unconsciously, like every man, he had pictured married life as the happiest enjoyment of love, with nothing to interfere and no petty worries to distract. He would, as he saw the arrangement, do his work, and find his rest from it in the happiness of love. She would be loved, and nothing more. But, like every man, he forgot that she too would want work. And it surprised him that she, his poetic, exquisite Kitty, could, not merely in the first weeks but in the first days of married life, think, remember, and busy herself about tablecloths and furniture, about mattresses for guests, about a tray, about the cook and dinner, and so on and on. While they were still engaged he had been struck by the firmness with which she had refused a trip abroad and chosen to go straight to the country, as though she already knew there was something she wanted, and could still think of something outside her love. That had jarred on him then, and now her trivial cares and worries jarred on him several times. But he saw that they were essential to her. And loving her as he did, although he didn't understand the reason for them and made fun of these domestic pursuits, he couldn't help admiring them. He made fun of the way she arranged the furniture they had brought from Moscow; reorganized their room; hung curtains; prepared rooms for guests; a room for Dolly; arranged a place for her new maid; gave dinner orders to the old cook; clashed with Agafea Mihalovna, taking the keys to the stores out of her hands. He saw how the old cook smiled, admiring her, and listened to her inexperienced, impossible orders, and how mournfully and tenderly Agafea Mihalovna shook her head over the young mistress's new arrangements. He saw that Kitty was extraordinarily sweet when, half laughing and half crying, she came to tell him that her maid, Masha, was used to thinking of her as her young lady, and so no one obeyed her. It seemed sweet to him, but strange, and he thought it would have been better without all of this.

He didn't know how great a sense of change she was going through; she, who at home had sometimes wanted some favorite dish, or some sweets, without any chance of getting either, could now order whatever she liked, buy pounds of sweets, spend as much money as she pleased, and order any pudding she fancied.

She was dreaming with delight now of Dolly arriving with her children, especially because she would order the children their favorite puddings, and Dolly would notice all her new housekeeping. She didn't herself know exactly why, but arranging her house had an irresistible pull for her. Instinctively sensing the approach of spring, and knowing that there would also be days of rough weather, she was building her nest as best she could, and was in a hurry both to build it and to learn how.

This concern for domestic details in Kitty, so opposed to Levin's idea of exalted happiness, was at first one of his disappointments; and this sweet busying with her household, the point of which he didn't understand but couldn't help loving, was one of his new happy surprises.

Another disappointment and happy surprise came with their quarrels. Levin could never have conceived that between him and his wife any other kind of relations could spring up than tender, respectful, loving ones, and all at once, in those very first days, they quarreled, so that she told him he did not care for her, that he cared for no one but himself, burst into tears, and wrung her hands.

This first quarrel arose from Levin going out to a new farmhouse and being half an hour too long getting back, because he had tried a shortcut home and had lost his way. He drove home thinking of nothing but her, of her love, of his own happiness, and the closer he got to home, the warmer his tenderness for her grew. He hurried into the room with the same feeling, with an even stronger feeling than he had had when he reached the Shtcherbatskys' house to make his proposal. And suddenly he was met by a darkened expression on her face that he had never seen before. He went to kiss her; she pushed him away.
"What is it?"

"You've been enjoying yourself," she began, trying to be calm and cutting. But the moment she opened her mouth, a torrent of reproach, of senseless jealousy, of everything that had been tormenting her during that half hour she had spent sitting motionless at the window burst out of her. It was only then, for the first time, that he clearly understood something he had not understood when he led her out of the church after the wedding. He felt now that he was not just close to her — that he no longer knew where he ended and she began. He felt it from the agonizing sense of being torn in two that he experienced at that instant. He was offended for the first second, but the very next second he felt that he could not be offended by her, that she was himself. He felt for the first moment what a man feels when, having suddenly taken a hard blow from behind, he turns around angry and ready to strike back, looking for his attacker, and finds it was himself who had hit himself by accident — that there is no one to be angry with, and that he must put up with the pain and try to soothe it.

Never afterwards did he feel it with the same intensity, but this first time he could not shake it for a long while. His natural impulse was to defend himself, to prove to her that she was wrong; but to prove her wrong would only mean irritating her further and widening the rift that was the cause of all his suffering. One habitual impulse pushed him to throw off the blame and pass it back to her. Another, stronger impulse pushed him to close the rift as quickly as possible without letting it grow. To stay under an undeserved reproach was wretched, but to make her suffer by justifying himself was worse still. Like a man half-awake in agony, he wanted to tear away the aching spot, to fling it off, and on coming to his senses he felt that the aching spot was himself. He could do nothing but try to help the aching spot bear it, and that was what he tried to do.

They made peace. She, realizing she was in the wrong, though she didn't say so, became tenderer to him, and they felt a new, redoubled happiness in their love. But that didn't keep such quarrels from happening again, very often too, on the most unexpected and trivial pretexts. These quarrels frequently sprang from the fact that they didn't yet know what mattered to each other, and that during this whole early period they were both often in a bad mood. When one was in a good mood and the other in a bad one, the peace held; but when both happened to be in a foul humor, quarrels would flare up over causes so incomprehensibly small that afterwards they could never remember what they had quarreled about. It is true that when they were both in good spirits their enjoyment of life was doubled. But still, this first period of their married life was a difficult one.

Through all this early time they had an unusually keen sense of tension, as if of a chain being tugged from both ends — the chain by which they were bound. All in all, their honeymoon — that is, the month following their wedding — from which by tradition Levin had expected so much, was not only not a time of sweetness but stayed in both their memories as the bitterest and most humiliating period of their lives. They each tried later on to scrub from memory all the monstrous, shameful incidents of that morbid time, when neither of them was often in a normal frame of mind, and neither was often quite themselves.
It was only in the third month of their marriage, after their return from Moscow, where they had been staying a month, that their life began to settle into a smoother rhythm.

title: Chapter 15
paragraphs: They had just come back from Moscow and were glad to be alone. He was sitting at the writing-table in his study, writing. She, in the dark lilac dress she had worn during the first days of their married life and had put on again today — a dress he particularly remembered and loved — was sitting on the sofa, the same old-fashioned leather sofa that had always stood in the study in Levin's father's and grandfather's day. She was sewing _broderie anglaise_. He was thinking and writing, never losing the happy awareness of her presence. His work, both on the land and on the book in which the principles of the new land system were to be set out, had not been dropped; but just as before these pursuits and ideas had seemed petty and trivial to him against the darkness that smothered all of life, now they seemed just as unimportant and small against the life that lay before him, lit by the brilliant light of happiness. He kept at his work, but he felt now that the center of gravity of his attention had shifted to something else, and that as a result he looked at his work in a different and clearer light. Before, this work had been an escape from life. Before, he had felt that without it his life would be too bleak. Now these pursuits were necessary so that his life would not be too uniformly bright. Picking up his manuscript, reading through what he had written, he was pleased to find that the work was worth working on. Many of his old ideas struck him as superfluous and extreme, but many gaps came clearly into view when he reviewed the whole thing in his memory. He was now writing a new chapter on the causes of the present disastrous state of agriculture in Russia. He argued that Russian poverty came not just from the anomalous distribution of landed property and misguided reforms, but that what had compounded the problem in recent years was the civilization grafted on from outside in an abnormal way — especially the rapid spread of communications such as railways, which led to the centralization in towns, the rise of luxury and, with it, the rise of manufacturing, of credit, and of the speculation that always tags along — all to the detriment of agriculture. It seemed to him that in a healthy buildup of national wealth all these phenomena would emerge only once a substantial amount of labor had been poured into agriculture, once it had come under settled, or at least defined, conditions; that a country's wealth ought to grow proportionally, and above all in such a way that no other source of wealth should outpace agriculture; that in step with a given level of agriculture there should be a corresponding level of transport; and that in our unsettled state of the land, railways, called into existence by political rather than economic needs, were premature, and instead of supporting agriculture, as expected, were competing with it and driving the growth of manufacturing and credit, and so stalling its progress; and that just as the one-sided, premature development of one organ in an animal would hinder the development of the whole, so in the overall growth of wealth in Russia, credit, transport, and manufacturing — necessary in Europe, where they had arisen at the right time — had with us done only harm, by pushing aside the chief question that needed settling: the question of how to organize agriculture.

While he was writing out his ideas, she was thinking how unnaturally cordial her husband had been to young Prince Tcharsky, who had, with great tactlessness, flirted with her the day before they left Moscow. "He's jealous," she thought. "Goodness! How sweet and silly he is! He's jealous of me! If he knew that I think no more of them than I do of Piotr the cook," she thought, looking at his head and red neck with a sense of ownership new even to her. "Although it's a shame to take him away from his work (but he has plenty of time!), I must look at his face; will he feel me looking at him? I want him to turn around ... I'll _will_ him to!" and she opened her eyes wide, as if to intensify the force of her gaze.
"Yes, they draw off all the sap and give a false appearance of prosperity," he muttered, stopping mid-sentence, and, feeling that she was watching him and smiling, he looked around.
"Well?" he asked, smiling, getting up.
"He looked round," she thought.
"It's nothing; I wanted you to look round," she said, watching him, trying to guess whether he was annoyed at being interrupted or not.
"How happy we are alone together! — I am, at any rate," he said, going over to her with a radiant smile of happiness.
"I'm just as happy. I'll never go anywhere, especially not to Moscow."
"And what were you thinking about?"
"Me? I was thinking.... No, no, go on, get back to writing; don't stop," she said, pursing her lips, "and I have to cut out these little holes now, you see?"
She picked up her scissors and started cutting them out.
"No; tell me, what was it?" he said, sitting down beside her and watching the tiny scissors going round.
"Oh! what was I thinking about? I was thinking about Moscow, about the back of your head."
"Why should I, of all people, have such happiness? It's unnatural, too good," he said, kissing her hand.
"I feel just the opposite; the better things are, the more natural it feels to me."
"And you've got a little curl loose," he said, carefully turning her head around.
"A little curl, oh yes. No, no, we're busy with our work!"
Work did not move forward, and they sprang apart from each other like guilty schoolchildren when Kouzma came in to announce that tea was ready.
"Have they come from town?" Levin asked Kouzma.
"They've just come; they're unpacking the things."
"Come quickly," she said to him as she went out of the study, "or else I'll read your letters without you."

Left alone, after putting his manuscripts together in the new portfolio she had bought him, he washed his hands at the new washstand with its elegant fittings — all of which had appeared along with her. Levin smiled at his own thoughts, and shook his head disapprovingly at those same thoughts; something like remorse was nagging at him. There was something shameful, effeminate, Capuan, as he called it to himself, in his current way of life. "It's not right to go on like this," he thought. "It will soon be three months, and I'm doing next to nothing. Today, almost for the first time, I sat down to serious work, and what happened? I did nothing but make a start and then push it aside. Even my usual occupations I've practically given up. I hardly walk or drive about the land anymore to check on things. Either I don't want to leave her, or I see she's bored on her own. And to think I used to suppose that before marriage life was hardly real, didn't really count, and that after marriage life began for good. And here almost three months have gone by and I've spent my time idly and uselessly. No, this won't do; I must start. Of course it's not her fault. She's not to blame in any way. I should have been firmer myself, kept my masculine independence; otherwise I'll fall into these habits, and so will she.... Of course she's not to blame," he told himself.

But it is hard for anyone who is dissatisfied not to blame somebody else, and especially the person nearest of all to him, for the cause of his dissatisfaction. And it vaguely crossed Levin's mind that she herself was not to blame (she could not be to blame for anything), but what was to blame was her education, too shallow and frivolous. ("That fool Tcharsky: she wanted to stop him, I know, but didn't know how.") "Yes, apart from her interest in the house (which she does have), apart from clothes and _broderie anglaise_, she has no serious interests. No interest in her work, in the estate, in the peasants, no interest in music, though she's rather good at it, no interest in reading. She does nothing, and is perfectly content." Levin, in his heart, judged her for this, and did not yet understand that she was getting herself ready for that period of activity that was coming for her, when she would be at once a wife to her husband and the mistress of the household, and would carry, nurse, and bring up children. He didn't know that she was instinctively aware of this, and, preparing herself for that time of overwhelming labor, did not reproach herself for the moments of carelessness and happiness in her love that she enjoyed now while cheerfully building her nest for the future.

title: Chapter 16
paragraphs: When Levin came upstairs, his wife was sitting beside the new silver samovar behind the new tea service, and, having settled old Agafea Mihalovna at a small table with a full cup of tea, was reading a letter from Dolly, with whom she was in constant correspondence.
"You see, your good lady's settled me here, told me to sit with her a bit," said Agafea Mihalovna, smiling affectionately at Kitty.

In those words of Agafea Mihalovna, Levin read the final act of the drama that had been playing out lately between her and Kitty. He saw that, even though Agafea Mihalovna's feelings had been hurt by a new mistress taking the reins of the household out of her hands, Kitty had won her over and made her love her.

"Here, I opened your letter too," said Kitty, handing him a clumsily written letter. "It's from that woman, I think, your brother's...." she said. "I didn't read it through. This one's from my people, and from Dolly. Imagine! Dolly took Tanya and Grisha to a children's ball at the Sarmatskys': Tanya went as a French marquise."

But Levin wasn't listening. Flushing, he took the letter from Marya Nikolaevna, his brother's former mistress, and began to read. This was the second letter he had received from Marya Nikolaevna. In the first, Marya Nikolaevna had written that his brother had sent her away through no fault of hers and, with touching simplicity, had added that although she was in need again, she was asking for nothing and wanted nothing, and was only tormented by the thought that Nikolay Dmitrievitch would come to ruin without her, given the weak state of his health, and she begged his brother to look after him. Now she wrote in quite a different tone. She had found Nikolay Dmitrievitch, had patched things up with him again in Moscow, and had moved with him to a provincial town, where he had taken a post in the government service. But he had quarreled with the head official and was now on his way back to Moscow, only he had fallen so ill on the road that it was doubtful whether he would ever leave his bed again, she wrote. "He has been talking about you the whole time, and besides, he has no money left."
"Read this; Dolly's writing about you," Kitty was starting, with a smile; but she broke off, noticing the changed look on her husband's face.
"What is it? What's wrong?"
"She writes that Nikolay, my brother, is at death's door. I'm going to him."
Kitty's face changed instantly. Thoughts of Tanya as a marquise, of Dolly — all gone.
"When are you leaving?" she said.
"Tomorrow."
"And I'm coming with you, all right?" she said.
"Kitty! What are you thinking of?" he said reproachfully.
"What do you mean?" — offended that he seemed to take her offer reluctantly and with irritation. "Why shouldn't I go? I won't be in your way. I...."
"I'm going because my brother is dying," said Levin. "Why should you...."
"Why? For the same reason as you."
"And, in a moment of such gravity for me, all she can think about is being bored on her own," Levin thought. And this lack of openness in such a serious moment infuriated him.
"It's out of the question," he said sternly.

Agafea Mihalovna, seeing that it was heading toward a quarrel, quietly set down her cup and slipped out. Kitty didn't even notice her. The tone in which her husband had said those last words stung her, especially because he clearly did not believe what she had told him.
"I'm telling you, if you go, I'm coming with you; I'm definitely coming," she said, quickly and angrily. "Why is it out of the question? Why do you say it's out of the question?"
"Because it's going God knows where, on all sorts of roads and into all sorts of hotels. You would be a hindrance to me," said Levin, trying to stay cool.
"Not at all. I don't need anything. Where you can go, I can...."
"Well, for one thing, because that woman is there — and you can't be in the same room with her."
"I don't know and I don't care to know who's there or what. I know that my husband's brother is dying and my husband is going to him, and I am going with my husband...."

"Kitty! Don't get angry. But think for a moment: this is something so serious that I can't stand the thought that you would mix in a feeling of weakness, of not wanting to be left alone. Look, you'll be lonely on your own, so go and spend a little while in Moscow."

"There — you always read base, ugly motives into me," she said, with tears of wounded pride and fury. "I didn't mean — it wasn't weakness, it wasn't ... I feel that it's my duty to be with my husband when he's in trouble, and you're trying on purpose to hurt me, you're trying on purpose not to understand...."
"No — this is unbearable! To be such a slave!" Levin cried, getting up, unable to hold his anger in any longer. But at the very same second he felt that he was beating himself.
"Then why did you marry? You could have stayed free. Why did you, if you regret it?" she said, getting up and running off into the drawing room.
When he came in to her, she was sobbing.

He began to speak, searching for words not to argue her out of it but simply to calm her. But she did not listen and would not agree to anything. He bent down to her and took her hand; it resisted him. He kissed her hand, kissed her hair, kissed her hand again — still she was silent. But when he took her face in both his hands and said "Kitty!" she suddenly came back to herself and started crying, and they were reconciled.

It was decided that they would leave together the next day. Levin told his wife that he believed she wanted to come simply to be useful, and agreed that Marya Nikolaevna's being with his brother did not make her going improper, but he set off, at the bottom of his heart, dissatisfied both with her and with himself. He was dissatisfied with her for being unable to bring herself to let him go when he had to (and how strange it felt to him that he, who had so recently barely dared to believe in such happiness as her loving him, was now unhappy because she loved him too much!), and he was dissatisfied with himself for not showing more strength of will. Even deeper was the sense of disagreement, at the bottom of his heart, about her not needing to take any account of the woman who was with his brother, and he thought with horror of all the situations they might run into. The mere idea of his wife, his Kitty, being in the same room as a common wench set him shuddering with horror and disgust.

title: Chapter 17
paragraphs: The hotel of the provincial town where Nikolay Levin lay ill was one of those provincial hotels built on the newest model of modern conveniences, with the best intentions of cleanliness, comfort, and even elegance, but, thanks to the kind of public that uses them, transformed with astonishing speed into filthy taverns with a pretension to modern improvement that only makes them worse than the old-fashioned, frankly filthy hotels. This one had already reached that stage, and the soldier in a grimy uniform smoking in the entryway, who was supposed to pass for a doorman, and the cast-iron, slippery, dark, unpleasant staircase, and the over-familiar waiter in a filthy frock coat, and the common dining room with a dusty bouquet of wax flowers on the table, and the filth, the dust, the disorder everywhere — combined with the kind of modern, up-to-date, self-satisfied railway-age fussiness of the place — gave Levin a particularly painful sensation after their fresh young life, especially because the false impression the hotel projected was so out of keeping with what awaited them.

As is always the case, after they had been asked what kind of room they wanted, it turned out that there was not a single decent room for them; one decent room had been taken by the inspector of railroads, another by a lawyer from Moscow, a third by Princess Astafieva from the country. There was only one filthy room left, next to which they promised another would come free by the evening. Annoyed with his wife because what he had foreseen had come about — that at the moment of arrival, when his heart was pounding with emotion and anxiety about his brother, he should have to be looking after her instead of rushing straight to him — Levin took her to the room they had been given.
"Go, go on!" she said, looking at him with timid, guilty eyes.

He walked out of the door without a word and at once almost ran into Marya Nikolaevna, who had heard of his arrival and hadn't dared come in to see him. She was just the same as when he had seen her in Moscow: the same woolen gown, the same bare arms and neck, the same good-naturedly stupid, pockmarked face, only a little plumper.
"Well, how is he? how is he?"
"Very bad. He can't get up. He has been waiting for you. He.... Are you ... with your wife?"
Levin did not at first understand what was confusing her, but she set him straight at once.
"I'll go away. I'll go down to the kitchen," she got out. "Nikolay Dmitrievitch will be glad. He heard about it, and remembers your lady, knew her abroad."
Levin realized she meant his wife, and didn't know what to say.
"Come, come to him!" he said.

But just as he started to move, the door of his room opened and Kitty looked out. Levin flushed with both shame and anger at his wife for putting herself and him in such an awkward position; but Marya Nikolaevna flushed even more. She practically shrank into herself, went red to the point of tears, and, clutching the ends of her apron in both hands, twisted them in her red fingers, not knowing what to say or do.
For the first instant Levin saw a look of eager curiosity in the eyes with which Kitty looked at this awful woman, so incomprehensible to her; but it lasted only a moment.
"Well! how is he?" she said, turning first to her husband and then to her.
"But we can't go on talking in the corridor like this!" Levin said, looking angrily at a gentleman who at that instant strolled jauntily down the hall, as though about his business.

"Well then, come in," said Kitty, turning to Marya Nikolaevna, who had pulled herself together; but, noticing her husband's appalled face, she added, "or go on; go, and then come back for me," and went back into the room.

Levin went to his brother's room. He had not at all expected what he saw and felt there. He had expected to find him in the same state of self-deception that he had heard was so common with consumptives, and that had struck him so much during his brother's visit in the autumn. He had expected to find the physical signs of the approach of death more marked — greater weakness, greater wasting — but otherwise much the same picture. He had expected to feel the same anguish at the loss of the brother he loved, the same horror in the face of death as he had felt then, only stronger. And he had braced himself for that; but he found something altogether different.

In a small dirty room with painted wall panels filthy with spittle, with voices audible through the thin partition from the next room, in a suffocating air saturated with impurities, on a bed pulled out from the wall, there lay, under a quilt, a body. One arm of this body was on top of the quilt, and the wrist, huge as a rake handle, was attached, somehow inconceivably, to the thin, long bone of the arm, smooth from the start of it to the middle. The head lay on its side on the pillow. Levin could make out the scanty strands of hair wet with sweat at the temples and on the tense, transparent-looking forehead.

"It can't be that that fearful body was my brother Nikolay?" Levin thought. But he came closer, saw the face, and doubt was no longer possible. Despite the terrible change in the face, Levin had only to glance at those eager eyes raised at his approach, only to catch the faint movement of the mouth beneath the sticky mustache, to take in the dreadful truth that this corpse-like body was his living brother.

The shining eyes looked sternly and reproachfully at his brother as he came up. And immediately that glance set up a living connection between living men. Levin felt at once the reproach in the eyes fixed on him, and felt remorse over his own happiness.
When Konstantin took him by the hand, Nikolay smiled. The smile was faint, barely there, and in spite of it the stern look in the eyes did not change.
"You didn't expect to find me like this," he forced out.
"Yes ... no," said Levin, stumbling over his words. "How was it you didn't let me know earlier, at the time of my wedding? I was asking everywhere."

He had to talk to fill the silence, and he didn't know what to say, especially since his brother gave no answer and just stared, never lowering his eyes, evidently seeing through to the inner meaning of every word. Levin told his brother that his wife had come with him. Nikolay said he was glad, but added that he was afraid his condition would frighten her. A silence followed. Suddenly Nikolay stirred and started to say something. From the look on his face Levin expected something of unusual gravity and weight, but Nikolay began talking about his health. He found fault with the doctor, lamenting that he didn't have a famous Moscow doctor. Levin saw that he still had hope.
Catching the first pause, Levin got up, anxious to escape, even for a moment, from his unbearable feelings, and said he would go and fetch his wife.

"Very well, and I'll tell her to tidy up here. It's filthy and reeks here, I expect. Marya! clear up the room," the sick man said with effort. "Oh, and when you've cleared it up, go away yourself," he added, looking inquiringly at his brother.

Levin made no answer. Stepping out into the corridor, he stopped short. He had said he would fetch his wife, but now, taking stock of what he was feeling, he decided to try the opposite — to talk her out of going in to the sick man. "Why should she suffer the way I am suffering?" he thought.
"Well, how is he?" Kitty asked, her face frightened.
"Oh, it's awful, it's awful! What did you come for?" said Levin.
Kitty was silent for a few seconds, looking timidly and sorrowfully at her husband; then she came up to him and took him by the elbow with both hands.

"Kostya! take me to him; it will be easier for us to bear it together. Just take me, take me to him, please, and then go away," she said. "You must understand that for me to see you and not to see him is far more painful. In there I could be a help to you and to him. Please, let me!" she pleaded with her husband, as if the happiness of her life depended on it.
Levin was forced to agree, and, getting hold of himself, and by now completely forgetting about Marya Nikolaevna, he went back in to his brother with Kitty.

Stepping lightly and glancing continually at her husband, showing him a brave, sympathetic face, Kitty went into the sick room and, turning without hurry, soundlessly shut the door. With inaudible steps she went quickly to the sick man's bedside, and approaching from a side where he didn't have to turn his head, she immediately clasped the skeleton of his huge hand in her fresh young one, pressed it, and began speaking with that soft eagerness, sympathetic without being grating, that is peculiar to women.
"We met, although we weren't introduced, at Soden," she said. "You never imagined I was to be your sister?"
"You wouldn't have recognized me?" he said, a radiant smile breaking out on his face at her arrival.
"Yes, I would have. What a good thing you let us know! Not a day has gone by without Kostya mentioning you, worrying about you."
But the sick man's interest did not last long.
Before she had finished speaking, the stern, reproachful look — the look of the dying man's envy of the living — had come back into his face.

"I'm afraid you're not quite comfortable here," she said, turning away from his fixed stare and glancing around the room. "We'll have to ask about another room," she said to her husband, "so we can be nearer."

title: Chapter 18
paragraphs: Levin could not look at his brother calmly; he could not be natural and calm in his presence. When he went in to the sick man, his eyes and his attention went unconsciously dim, and he did not see and did not register the details of his brother's situation. He smelled the awful odor, saw the dirt, the disorder, the wretched state of things, and heard the groans, and felt that nothing could be done to help. It did not occur to him to analyze the details of the sick man's situation, to consider how that body was lying under the quilt, how those wasted legs and thighs and spine were huddled, and whether they could not be arranged more comfortably, whether something might be done to make things, if not better, at least less bad. It made his blood run cold the moment he began to think about any of these details. He was absolutely certain that nothing could be done to prolong his brother's life or to relieve his suffering. But the sick man could feel that his brother regarded all help as out of the question, and it exasperated him. And that made it more painful still for Levin. To be in the sick room was agony to him; not to be there was worse. So he was constantly slipping out, on one pretext or another, and coming back in, because he couldn't bear to be alone.

But Kitty thought, and felt, and acted quite differently. The moment she saw the sick man, she pitied him. And pity, in her womanly heart, did not stir up the horror and disgust it had stirred up in her husband; instead it raised a desire to act, to find out every detail of his condition and to do something about it. And since she had not the slightest doubt that it was her duty to help him, she had no doubt either that it was possible, and she got to work at once. The very details, the mere thought of which had reduced her husband to terror, immediately had her attention. She sent for the doctor, sent to the chemist's, set the maid she had brought with her and Marya Nikolaevna to sweeping and dusting and scrubbing; she herself washed one thing, rinsed out another, tucked something under the quilt. Something was, on her instructions, brought into the sick room, something else was carried out. She herself went several times to her own room, paying no attention to the men she passed in the corridor, getting out and bringing back sheets, pillowcases, towels, shirts.

The waiter, who was occupied with a party of engineers dining in the dining hall, came up several times with an irritated look in answer to her bell, but couldn't avoid carrying out her orders, since she gave them with such gracious insistence that there was no getting around her. Levin disapproved of all this; he didn't believe any of it would do the patient any good. Above all, he was afraid the patient would be angered by it. But the sick man, although he seemed and was indifferent to it, was not angered, only abashed, and on the whole, as it were, intrigued by what she was doing with him. Coming back from the doctor Kitty had sent him to, Levin opened the door and walked in just as, by Kitty's orders, they were changing the patient's linen. The long white ridge of his spine, with the huge, protruding shoulder blades and jutting ribs and vertebrae, was bare, and Marya Nikolaevna and the waiter were struggling with the sleeve of the nightshirt, unable to get the long, limp arm into it. Kitty, quickly shutting the door behind Levin, was not looking that way; but the sick man groaned, and she moved toward him at once.
"Hurry," she said.
"Oh, don't you come here," the sick man said angrily. "I'll do it myself...."
"What did he say?" Marya Nikolaevna asked. But Kitty had heard, and saw that he was ashamed and uncomfortable at being naked in front of her.
"I'm not looking, I'm not looking!" she said, slipping the arm in. "Marya Nikolaevna, come around this side, you do it," she added.

"Please go and get something for me — there's a little bottle in my small bag," she said, turning to her husband, "you know, in the side pocket; bring it, please, and in the meantime they'll finish clearing up here."

Returning with the bottle, Levin found the sick man settled comfortably and everything around him completely transformed. The heavy smell had been replaced by the smell of aromatic vinegar, which Kitty, with pursed lips and puffed-out, rosy cheeks, was squirting through a little pipe. There was no dust visible anywhere; a rug had been put down beside the bed. On the table the medicine bottles and decanters were tidily arranged, and the linen they needed was folded up there, along with Kitty's _broderie anglaise_. On the other table by the patient's bed there were candles and drink and powders. The sick man himself, washed and combed, lay between clean sheets on high pillows, in a clean nightshirt with a white collar around his astonishingly thin neck, and with a new expression of hope he kept his eyes fixed on Kitty.

The doctor Levin had brought, found at the club, was not the one who had been attending Nikolay Levin, since the patient was dissatisfied with that one. The new doctor took up a stethoscope and sounded the patient, shook his head, prescribed medicine, and with extreme thoroughness explained first how to take the medicine and then what diet should be kept to. He recommended eggs, raw or only lightly cooked, and seltzer water, with warm milk at a particular temperature. When the doctor had gone, the sick man said something to his brother, of which Levin could make out only the last words: "Your Katya." From the look with which he gazed at her, Levin saw that he was praising her. He called her Katya, in fact, as he had begun to call her.

"I'm much better already," he said. "Why, with you here I'd have been well again long ago. How good this is!" He took her hand and drew it toward his lips, but, as though afraid it would disgust her, he changed his mind, let it go, and only stroked it. Kitty took his hand in both of hers and pressed it.
"Now turn me over on the left side, and go to bed," he said.
No one could make out what he was saying except Kitty; she alone understood him. She understood him because she was mentally keeping watch the whole time over what he needed.
"On the other side," she said to her husband, "he always sleeps on that side. Turn him over, it's so unpleasant calling the servants. I'm not strong enough. Can you?" she said to Marya Nikolaevna.
"I'm afraid not," Marya Nikolaevna answered.

Terrifying as it was to Levin to put his arms around that terrifying body, to take hold of that thing under the quilt, of which he would have preferred to know nothing, he put on, under his wife's influence, the resolute face she knew so well, and, sliding his arms into the bed, took hold of the body — and, in spite of his own strength, was struck by the strange heaviness of those helpless limbs. While he was turning him over, conscious of the huge wasted arm around his neck, Kitty swiftly and noiselessly turned the pillow, beat it out and arranged in it the sick man's head, smoothing back the hair that was sticking again to his damp forehead.

The sick man kept his brother's hand in his own. Levin felt that he meant to do something with his hand and was pulling it toward something. Levin yielded with a sinking heart: yes, he drew it to his mouth and kissed it. Levin, shaking with sobs and unable to get out a word, walked out of the room.

title: Chapter 19
paragraphs: "Thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes." That was what Levin thought about his wife as he talked to her that evening.

Levin was thinking of the verse not because he considered himself "wise and prudent." He didn't consider himself that, but he couldn't help knowing that he had more intellect than his wife and Agafea Mihalovna, and he couldn't help knowing that when he thought about death, he thought with the full force of his intellect. He knew, too, that the minds of many great men, whose thoughts he had read, had brooded over death and still had not known a hundredth of what his wife and Agafea Mihalovna knew about it. Different as those two women were, Agafea Mihalovna and Katya, as his brother Nikolay had called her, and as Levin particularly liked to call her now, they were entirely alike in this. Both knew, without a shadow of doubt, what life was and what death was, and although neither of them could have answered, or even understood, the questions that Levin was wrestling with, both had no doubt of the meaning of this event, and both looked at it in exactly the same way — a way shared with millions of other people. The proof that they knew with certainty the nature of death lay in the fact that they knew without a moment's hesitation how to handle the dying, and were not afraid of them. Levin and other men like him, although they could have said a great deal about death, clearly did not know this, since they were afraid of death and at a complete loss as to what to do when people were dying. If Levin had been alone now with his brother Nikolay, he would have looked at him in terror, and waited in even greater terror, and not known what else to do.

More than that, he didn't know what to say, how to look, how to move. To talk of unrelated things felt to him shocking, impossible; to talk of death and gloomy subjects — also impossible. To be silent, also impossible. "If I look at him he'll think I'm studying him, that I'm afraid; if I don't look at him, he'll think I'm thinking about other things. If I walk on tiptoe, he'll be annoyed; to walk normally, I'm ashamed." Kitty clearly did not think about herself and had no time to think about herself: she was thinking about him, because she knew something, and everything went well. She told him about herself, even about her wedding, and smiled and sympathized with him and petted him, and talked about cases of recovery, and everything went well; so she must know. The proof that her behavior, and Agafea Mihalovna's, was not instinctive, animal, irrational, was that, in addition to the physical care and the relief of suffering, both Agafea Mihalovna and Kitty wanted something more important for the dying man than the physical care, something that had nothing in common with physical conditions. Agafea Mihalovna, speaking of a man who had just died, had said: "Well, thank God, he received the sacrament and the absolution; God grant each of us such a death." Katya, in just the same way, on top of all her concern about linen, bedsores, drink, found time, on the very first day, to convince the sick man of the need to receive the sacrament and absolution.

When they got back from the sick room to their own two rooms for the night, Levin sat with his head hanging, not knowing what to do. Never mind supper, getting ready for bed, planning what they were going to do — he could not even talk to his wife; he was ashamed to. Kitty, by contrast, was busier than usual. She was even livelier than usual. She ordered supper to be brought up, unpacked their things herself, helped to make the beds, and didn't even forget to sprinkle them with Persian powder. She showed the kind of alertness, that quickness of mind, that comes out in men before a battle, in conflict, in the dangerous and decisive moments of life — those moments when a man shows once and for all what he is worth, and that all his past has not been wasted but has been preparation for these moments.

Everything sped along in her hands, and before twelve o'clock had struck, all their things were arranged neatly and cleanly in her rooms, in such a way that the hotel rooms felt like home: the beds were made, brushes, combs, mirrors were laid out, table napkins were spread.

Levin felt that even now to eat, to sleep, to talk was unpardonable, and it seemed to him that every move he made was unseemly. She arranged the brushes, but she did it all in such a way that there was nothing shocking in it.
Neither of them could eat, however, and for a long while they couldn't sleep, and they didn't even go to bed.

"I'm very glad I persuaded him to receive extreme unction tomorrow," she said, sitting in her dressing jacket in front of her folding mirror, combing her soft, fragrant hair with a fine comb. "I've never seen it, but I know — mamma told me — there are prayers said for recovery."
"Do you really suppose he might recover?" said Levin, watching a slender strand at the back of her small round head that kept disappearing when she drew the comb through from the front.

"I asked the doctor; he said he couldn't live more than three days. But how can they be sure? I'm very glad, anyway, that I persuaded him," she said, glancing sideways at her husband through her hair. "Anything is possible," she added, with that peculiar, slightly sly expression that was always on her face when she spoke about religion.

Since their conversation about religion when they were engaged, neither of them had ever started up a discussion of the subject, but she went through all the ceremonies of going to church, saying her prayers, and so on, always with the unwavering conviction that it ought to be that way. In spite of his claims to the contrary, she was firmly convinced that he was as much a Christian as she was, and indeed a far better one; and everything he said about it was simply one of his ridiculous masculine quirks, just like what he would say about her _broderie anglaise_, that good people patch holes, but that she cut them on purpose, and so on.

"Yes, you see this woman, Marya Nikolaevna, didn't know how to manage any of this," said Levin. "And ... I have to admit I'm very, very glad you came. You're such purity that...." He took her hand and didn't kiss it (to kiss her hand so close to death felt to him improper); he only squeezed it with a repentant air, looking at her brightening eyes.

"It would have been miserable for you to be alone," she said, and, lifting her hands which had hidden her cheeks flushing with pleasure, she twisted the coil of her hair on the nape of her neck and pinned it in place. "No," she went on, "she didn't know how to.... Luckily, I picked up a lot at Soden."
"Are there really people there as ill as this?"
"Worse."
"What I find so awful is that I can't see him as he was when he was young. You wouldn't believe how charming he was as a young man, but I didn't understand him then."
"I can — I really can believe it. How I feel that we might have been friends!" she said; and, distressed at what she had just said, she glanced over at her husband, and tears came into her eyes.
"Yes, _might have been_," he said sadly. "He's just one of those people of whom they say they're not for this world."
"But we have many days ahead of us; we should go to bed," said Kitty, glancing at her tiny watch.

title: Chapter 20
paragraphs: The next day the sick man received the sacrament and extreme unction. During the ceremony Nikolay Levin prayed fervently. His great eyes, fixed on the holy image set out on a card table covered with a colored napkin, expressed such passionate prayer and hope that it was painful for Levin to watch. Levin knew that this passionate prayer and hope would only make parting from the life he loved so much more bitter. Levin knew his brother and how his mind worked: he knew that his unbelief had come about not because life was easier for him without faith, but because step by step the modern scientific account of natural phenomena had crushed out the possibility of faith for him; and so he knew that this present return was not a legitimate one, brought about by the same workings of his intellect, but simply a temporary, self-interested return to faith in a desperate hope of recovery. Levin knew, too, that Kitty had strengthened his hope with stories of the marvelous recoveries she had heard about. Levin knew all this; and it was agonizingly painful for him to watch the pleading, hopeful eyes, the wasted wrist lifted with difficulty as it made the sign of the cross over the tense forehead, the prominent shoulders and the hollow, gasping chest, which one could not square with the life the sick man was praying for. During the sacrament Levin did what he, an unbeliever, had done a thousand times. He said, addressing God, "If Thou dost exist, make this man to recover" (this same thing, of course, has been repeated many times), "and Thou wilt save him and me."

After extreme unction the sick man suddenly became much better. He did not cough once in the course of an hour, smiled, kissed Kitty's hand thanking her with tears, and said he was comfortable, free of pain, and felt strong and had an appetite. He even sat up when his soup was brought, and asked for a cutlet besides. Hopelessly ill as he was, obvious as it was at a glance that he could not recover, Levin and Kitty were both for that hour in the same state of excitement, happy, though afraid of being mistaken.
"Is he better?"
"Yes, much."
"It's wonderful."
"There's nothing wonderful about it."
"Anyway, he's better," they said in a whisper, smiling at each other.

This self-deception did not last long. The sick man fell into a quiet sleep, but he was woken up half an hour later by his cough. And all at once every hope vanished in those around him and in himself. The reality of his suffering crushed every hope in Levin and Kitty and in the sick man himself, leaving no doubt, not even a memory of past hopes.

Without referring to what he had believed half an hour before, as though ashamed even to recall it, he asked for iodine to inhale in a bottle covered with perforated paper. Levin handed him the bottle, and the same look of passionate hope with which he had taken the sacrament was now fixed on his brother, demanding from him confirmation of the doctor's claim that inhaling iodine worked wonders.

"Is Katya not here?" he gasped, looking around while Levin reluctantly agreed with the doctor's words. "No; then I can say it.... It was for her sake I went through that farce. She's so sweet; but you and I can't fool ourselves. This is what I believe in," he said, and, squeezing the bottle in his bony hand, he began breathing over it.

At eight o'clock in the evening Levin and his wife were drinking tea in their room when Marya Nikolaevna ran in, out of breath. She was pale, and her lips were trembling. "He's dying!" she whispered. "I'm afraid he'll go this minute."
Both of them rushed in to him. He was sitting propped up on one elbow on the bed, his long back bent, his head hanging low.
"How do you feel?" Levin asked in a whisper, after a silence.

"I feel I'm setting off," Nikolay said with difficulty, but with extreme clarity, forcing the words out of himself. He did not raise his head, but only turned his eyes upward without their reaching his brother's face. "Katya, go away!" he added.
Levin jumped up, and with a sharp whisper made her leave the room.
"I'm setting off," he said again.
"Why do you say that?" said Levin, just to say something.
"Because I'm setting off," he repeated, as if the phrase pleased him. "It's the end."
Marya Nikolaevna went over to him.
"You'd better lie down; you'd be more comfortable," she said.
"I'll lie down soon enough," he said slowly, "when I'm dead," he added, sarcastically, furiously. "Well, you can lay me down if you like."

Levin laid his brother on his back, sat down beside him, and watched his face, holding his breath. The dying man lay with closed eyes, but from time to time the muscles in his forehead twitched, as in someone thinking deeply and intently. Levin involuntarily thought along with him about what was happening to him now, but, in spite of all his mental effort to follow him, he saw from the look on that calm, stern face that for the dying man everything was growing clearer and clearer, while for Levin it was as dark as it had always been.

"Yes, yes, so," the dying man got out slowly, at intervals. "Wait a little." He fell silent. "Right!" he said suddenly, in a reassuring tone, as if everything were now resolved for him. "O Lord!" he murmured, and sighed deeply.
Marya Nikolaevna felt his feet. "They're getting cold," she whispered.

For a long while, a very long while it seemed to Levin, the sick man lay motionless. But he was still alive, and from time to time he sighed. By now Levin was worn out from the mental strain. He felt that, with no mental effort, could he grasp what it was that was _right_. He could not even think about the problem of death itself, but, without his choosing it, thoughts kept rising in him of what he would have to do next: closing the dead man's eyes, dressing him, ordering the coffin. And, strange to say, he felt utterly cold, and was conscious of no grief and no sense of loss, still less of any pity for his brother. If he felt anything for his brother at that moment, it was envy of the knowledge the dying man now possessed and he could not.

He sat over him for a long while like this, expecting the end at any moment. But the end did not come. The door opened, and Kitty appeared. Levin got up to stop her. But at the moment he was getting up, he caught the sound of the dying man stirring.
"Don't go away," Nikolay said, and held out his hand. Levin gave him his own, and waved angrily at his wife to leave.

With the dying man's hand in his, he sat for half an hour, an hour, another hour. He didn't think of death at all now. He was wondering what Kitty was doing; who was staying in the next room; whether the doctor had a house of his own. He was hungry and sleepy. He cautiously drew his hand away and felt the feet. The feet were cold, but the sick man was still breathing. Levin tried again to step away on tiptoe, but the sick man stirred again and said: "Don't go."

Dawn came; the sick man's condition was unchanged. Levin quietly withdrew his hand and, without looking at the dying man, went off to his own room and fell asleep. When he woke up, instead of news of his brother's death, which he had expected, he learned that the sick man had returned to his earlier condition. He had begun sitting up again, coughing, eating again, talking again, and had once more stopped speaking of death, had once more begun to express hope of recovery, and had become more irritable and gloomier than ever. No one — neither his brother nor Kitty — could soothe him. He was angry with everyone, said nasty things to everyone, blamed everyone for his suffering, and insisted they should bring him a famous doctor from Moscow. To every inquiry about how he felt he gave the same answer with an expression of vindictive reproach: "I'm suffering horribly, intolerably!"

The sick man was suffering more and more, especially from bedsores, which by now could not be helped, and he grew angrier and angrier with everyone around him, blaming them for everything, and especially for not having brought him a doctor from Moscow. Kitty tried every possible way to ease him, to soothe him; but it was all in vain, and Levin saw that she herself was exhausted both physically and morally, even though she would not admit it. The sense of death, which had been called up in all of them by his taking leave of life on the night when he had sent for his brother, had broken up. Everyone knew that he must inevitably die soon, that he was half-dead already. Everyone wished for nothing but that he would die as soon as possible, and everyone, hiding this, kept giving him medicines, kept hunting for remedies and doctors, and went on deceiving him and themselves and each other. All of it was lies — disgusting, irreverent deceit. And, because of the bent of his character, and because he loved the dying man more than anyone else did, Levin felt this deceit most painfully of all.

Levin, who had long been seized by the idea of reconciling his brothers, at least in the face of death, had written to his brother Sergey Ivanovitch, and, having received an answer, he read this letter aloud to the sick man. Sergey Ivanovitch wrote that he could not come himself, and in touching terms begged his brother's forgiveness.
The sick man said nothing.
"What am I to write to him?" said Levin. "I hope you aren't angry with him?"
"No, not in the least!" Nikolay answered, annoyed at the question. "Tell him to send me a doctor."

Three more days of agony followed; the sick man was still in the same condition. The wish for his death was now felt by everyone at the mere sight of him — by the waiters and the hotel-keeper and all the guests in the hotel, and by the doctor and Marya Nikolaevna and Levin and Kitty.
