Only the sick man himself did not express this feeling, but on the contrary was furious at their not bringing him doctors, and went on taking medicine and talking about life. Only at rare moments, when the opium gave him an instant's relief from the never-ending pain, he would sometimes, half asleep, let out what was more intense in his heart than in anyone else's: "Oh, if it were only the end!" or: "When will it be over?"

His sufferings, steadily growing more intense, did their work and prepared him for death. There was no position in which he was not in pain, no minute in which he was not aware of it, not a limb, not a part of his body that did not ache and torment him. Even the memories, the impressions, the thoughts attached to this body now woke in him the same revulsion as the body itself. The sight of other people, their words, his own recollections — everything was a source of agony for him. The people around him felt this, and instinctively held back from moving freely, from talking, from expressing their wishes in his presence. All his life was now reduced to a single feeling — suffering and the desire to be rid of it.

There was clearly coming over him that reversal that would make him see death as the goal of all his desires, as happiness. Up to now each particular desire, brought on by suffering or deprivation — hunger, fatigue, thirst — had been met by some bodily function that gave pleasure. But now no physical craving or pain was being relieved, and any effort to relieve them only caused fresh suffering. And so all his desires were folded into one — the desire to be rid of all his sufferings and of their source, the body. But he had no words for this desire of deliverance, and so he did not speak of it, and out of habit went on asking for the satisfaction of desires that could no longer be satisfied. "Turn me over on the other side," he would say, and immediately afterwards would ask to be turned back the way he had been. "Give me some broth. Take the broth away. Talk about something: why are you all silent?" And the moment they started to talk he would close his eyes and show weariness, indifference, loathing.
On the tenth day after their arrival in the town, Kitty was unwell. She had a headache and felt sick, and could not get up all morning.
The doctor said the indisposition came from exhaustion and emotional strain, and prescribed rest.

After dinner, however, Kitty got up and, as usual, went with her work to the sick man. He looked at her sternly when she came in, and smiled contemptuously when she said she had been unwell. That day he was constantly blowing his nose and groaning pitifully.
"How do you feel?" she asked him.
"Worse," he forced out. "In pain!"
"In pain, where?"
"Everywhere."

"It will be over today, you'll see," said Marya Nikolaevna. Though it was said in a whisper, the sick man, whose hearing Levin had noticed was very keen, must have heard. Levin shushed her and looked round at the sick man. Nikolay had heard; but these words had no effect on him. His eyes still held the same intense, reproachful look.
"Why do you think so?" Levin asked her, when she had followed him out into the corridor.
"He's started picking at himself," said Marya Nikolaevna.
"What do you mean?"
"Like this," she said, tugging at the folds of her woolen skirt. Levin noticed, in fact, that all that day the patient kept pulling at himself, as if trying to snatch something away.

Marya Nikolaevna's prediction came true. Toward night the sick man could no longer lift his hands, and could only gaze ahead of him with the same intensely concentrated expression in his eyes. Even when his brother or Kitty bent over him so that he could see them, he looked the same way. Kitty sent for the priest to read the prayer for the dying.

While the priest was reading it, the dying man showed no sign of life; his eyes were closed. Levin, Kitty, and Marya Nikolaevna stood by the bed. The priest had not quite finished reading the prayer when the dying man stretched, sighed, and opened his eyes. The priest, on finishing the prayer, put the cross to the cold forehead, then slowly returned it to the stand, and after standing two more minutes in silence, he touched the huge, bloodless hand that was turning cold.

"He is gone," said the priest, and would have moved off; but suddenly there was a faint stir in the dead man's mustaches, which seemed glued together, and quite distinctly, in the hush, they heard from the bottom of his chest the sharply defined sounds:
"Not quite ... soon."
And a minute later the face brightened, a smile came out under the mustaches, and the women who had gathered around began carefully laying out the corpse.

The sight of his brother, and the nearness of death, revived in Levin that sense of horror in the face of the insoluble enigma, together with the nearness and inevitability of death, that had come over him on that autumn evening when his brother had come to him. That feeling was even stronger now than before; even less than before did he feel capable of grasping the meaning of death, and its inevitability rose up before him more terrible than ever. But now, thanks to his wife's presence, that feeling did not drive him to despair. Despite death, he felt the need of life and love. He felt that love saved him from despair, and that this love, under the threat of despair, had become still stronger and purer. The one mystery of death, still unsolved, had barely passed before his eyes when another mystery had risen up, equally insoluble, urging him to love and to life.
The doctor confirmed his suppositions about Kitty. Her indisposition was a symptom that she was with child.

title: Chapter 21
paragraphs: From the moment Alexey Alexandrovitch grasped — from his conversations with Betsy and with Stepan Arkadyevitch — that all anyone expected of him was to leave his wife alone, not to burden her with his presence, and that his wife herself wanted this, he became so disoriented that he could not decide anything on his own. He no longer knew what he wanted, and so he handed himself over to the people who were so happy to take an interest in his affairs and agreed to whatever they proposed. Only when Anna had actually left the house, and the English governess sent up to ask whether she should dine with him or by herself, did he finally see his situation clearly — and the sight horrified him. The hardest part was that he could not connect his past with the present in any coherent way. It was not the earlier past, the years of happy life with his wife, that troubled him. He had already lived through, miserably, the shift from that past to the knowledge of her infidelity — a painful state, but one he could understand. If she had left him then, the moment she confessed, he would have been wounded and unhappy, but he would not have been in this hopeless, baffling position he was in now. He could not reconcile his recent past — his tenderness, his love for his sick wife, his love for another man's child — with the fact that, in return for all that, he now found himself alone, shamed, ridiculous, useful to no one and despised by everyone.

For the first two days after his wife was gone, Alexey Alexandrovitch went on as usual: he received people who came asking favors, met with his chief secretary, drove to the committee, came down to dine in the dining room. Without putting it to himself in so many words, he was straining every nerve for those two days simply to keep up the appearance of composure, even of indifference. When servants asked him what to do with Anna Arkadyevna's rooms and belongings, it cost him enormous effort to look like a man for whom none of this was unexpected or out of the ordinary, and he succeeded: no one could have spotted a sign of despair in him. But on the second day after she left, when Korney brought him a bill from a fashionable draper's shop that Anna had forgotten to pay, and reported that the clerk from the shop was waiting, Alexey Alexandrovitch told him to send the clerk up.
"Forgive me, your excellency, for troubling you. But if you direct us to apply to her excellency, would you be so good as to give us her address?"

Alexey Alexandrovitch seemed to pause and think, or so it looked to the clerk, and then suddenly turned and sat down at the table. He let his head sink into his hands and stayed that way for a long time. Several times he tried to speak and broke off. Korney, seeing his master's state, asked the clerk to come back another time. Left alone, Alexey Alexandrovitch realized he no longer had the strength to keep up the front of firmness and composure. He gave orders for the carriage that had been waiting to be sent back, said he would see no one, and did not go down to dinner.

He felt he could not endure the weight of contempt and irritation that he had clearly seen in the face of the clerk and of Korney and of everyone he had crossed paths with over those two days. He felt he could not deflect people's hatred from himself, because that hatred was not provoked by his being bad — if it had been, he could have tried to be better — but by his being shamefully and disgustingly unhappy. He knew that for this — for the very fact that his heart was torn open with grief — they would show him no mercy. He felt that people would crush him the way dogs strangle a wounded dog yelping in pain. He knew that his only safety against them was to hide his wounds, and he had tried to do that for two days by instinct, but now he could not keep up the lopsided fight any longer.

His despair was made worse by the awareness that he was completely alone in his grief. In all of Petersburg there was not a single person to whom he could speak about what he was feeling, who would feel for him not as a high official, not as a member of society, but simply as a man in pain; in fact he had no such person anywhere in the world.

Alexey Alexandrovitch had grown up an orphan. There had been two brothers. They did not remember their father, and their mother died when Alexey Alexandrovitch was ten. The estate was a small one. Their uncle Karenin, a senior government official who had at one time been a favorite of the late Tsar, had raised them.

Having finished high school and university with medals, Alexey Alexandrovitch, with his uncle's backing, stepped straight into a prominent position in the civil service and from then on dedicated himself entirely to political ambition. In high school, at university, and afterwards in the service, he had never formed a close friendship with anyone. The one person closest to his heart had been his brother, but his brother held a post in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and was permanently abroad, where he died not long after Alexey Alexandrovitch's marriage.

While he was governor of a province, Anna's aunt — a wealthy provincial lady — had thrown him together with her niece. He was already middle-aged, though young for a governor, and she contrived matters so that he had either to declare himself or to leave the town. Alexey Alexandrovitch did not deliberate long. There were as many reasons to do it as not to, and nothing strong enough to override his standing rule of abstaining when in doubt. But Anna's aunt, through a mutual acquaintance, hinted that he had already compromised the girl and was honor-bound to propose. So he proposed, and concentrated on his fiancée and then his wife every drop of feeling he was capable of.

His attachment to Anna ruled out, in his heart, any need for close ties with anyone else. And so among all his acquaintances he had not one real friend. He had plenty of so-called connections, but no friendships. He had any number of people he could invite to dinner, whose sympathy he could call on for some public matter he cared about, whose help he could count on for someone he wanted to assist, with whom he could frankly discuss other people's business or affairs of state. But his relations with these people ran along one well-defined channel and followed a routine he could not step outside of. There was one man, a university classmate, with whom he had grown closer later and to whom he might have spoken about a private sorrow — but that friend held a post in the Department of Education in a remote part of Russia. Of the people actually in Petersburg, the most intimate and the most plausible were his chief secretary and his doctor.

Mihail Vassilievitch Sludin, the chief secretary, was a straightforward, intelligent, kindhearted, and conscientious man, and Alexey Alexandrovitch knew that he wished him well personally. But five years of working together had built a barrier between them that ruled out anything warmer.

After signing the papers Sludin had brought, Alexey Alexandrovitch sat for a long while in silence, glancing at him, and several times opened his mouth to speak and couldn't. He had even prepared the phrase: "You have heard about my trouble?" But in the end he just said, as usual, "So you'll get this ready for me?" and dismissed him.
The other man was the doctor, who also felt kindly toward him; but it had long been silently understood between them that both were swamped with work and always in a hurry.
As for the women he knew, with Countess Lidia Ivanovna at the head of the list, Alexey Alexandrovitch never thought of them at all. Women, simply as women, were frightening and distasteful to him.

title: Chapter 22
paragraphs: Alexey Alexandrovitch had forgotten Countess Lidia Ivanovna, but she had not forgotten him. At the worst point of his lonely despair she came to him, and without waiting to be announced she walked straight into his study. She found him sitting with his head in both hands.

"_J'ai forcé la consigne_," she said, sweeping in with quick steps, breathing hard from excitement and the speed of her walk. "I have heard everything! Alexey Alexandrovitch! Dear friend!" she went on, warmly squeezing his hand in both of hers and gazing into his eyes with her fine, pensive ones.
Frowning, Alexey Alexandrovitch stood up, eased his hand free, and pulled a chair over for her.
"Won't you sit down, countess? I'm not receiving anyone — I'm unwell, countess," he said, and his lips twitched.

"Dear friend!" Countess Lidia Ivanovna repeated, not taking her eyes off his. Suddenly her eyebrows rose at the inner corners, making a triangle on her forehead; her plain yellow face grew plainer still — but Alexey Alexandrovitch could feel that she was sorry for him and on the verge of tears. He softened too; he grabbed her plump hand and started kissing it.
"Dear friend!" she said in a voice that cracked with feeling. "You must not give in to grief. Your sorrow is great, but you have to find consolation."

"I am crushed, I am annihilated, I am no longer a man!" said Alexey Alexandrovitch, letting go of her hand but still gazing into her brimming eyes. "My position is so terrible because I can find no support anywhere — not even inside myself."

"You will find support. Seek it — not in me, though I beg you to believe in my friendship," she said with a sigh. "Our support is love, the love He has granted us. His burden is light," she said, with that look of ecstasy Alexey Alexandrovitch knew well. "He will be your support and your help."

Although there was in these words a touch of that self-congratulatory emotion at her own elevated feelings, and of that new mystical fervor which had recently spread in Petersburg and which Alexey Alexandrovitch found overblown, it was still pleasant to him to hear it now.
"I am weak. I am crushed. I foresaw none of this, and now I understand none of it."
"Dear friend," Lidia Ivanovna repeated.

"It's not the loss of what I no longer have — it isn't that!" Alexey Alexandrovitch went on. "I don't grieve for that. But I cannot help feeling humiliated in front of other people for the position I'm in. It's wrong, but I can't help it, I can't help it."

"That noble act of forgiveness was not performed by you — it was done through you. I was moved to ecstasy by it, and so was everyone else. He was working inside your heart," said Countess Lidia Ivanovna, lifting her eyes rapturously, "and so you cannot be ashamed of what you did."
Alexey Alexandrovitch knit his brows and, bending his fingers back, cracked his knuckles.

"One has to know all the facts," he said in his thin voice. "A man's strength has its limits, countess, and I have reached mine. The whole day I have been having to make arrangements — household arrangements arising" (he stressed the word _arising_) "from my new, solitary position. The servants, the governess, the accounts.... These pinpricks have stabbed me to the heart, and I do not have the strength to bear it. At dinner ... yesterday, I was almost ready to get up from the table. I could not stand the way my son looked at me. He did not ask what any of it meant, but he wanted to, and I could not bear the look in his eyes. He was afraid to look at me, but that is not all...." Alexey Alexandrovitch would have mentioned the bill that had been brought to him, but his voice shook and he stopped. He could not think of that bill on blue paper, for a hat and ribbons, without a wave of self-pity.

"I understand, dear friend," said Lidia Ivanovna. "I understand all of it. Help and comfort you will not find in me, though I have come precisely in order to help if I can. If only I could lift these petty, humiliating cares off you.... I understand that a woman's word, a woman's supervision is needed. Will you entrust it to me?"
Silently and gratefully Alexey Alexandrovitch pressed her hand.
"Together we will look after Seryozha. Practical matters are not my strong suit. But I will get to work. I will be your housekeeper. Don't thank me. I am not doing it on my own account...."
"I cannot help thanking you."

"But, dear friend, do not give in to that feeling you spoke of — being ashamed of what is the Christian's highest glory: _he who humbles himself shall be exalted_. And you cannot thank me. You must thank Him, and pray to Him for help. In Him alone we find peace, consolation, salvation, and love," she said, and turning her eyes upward, she began to pray, as Alexey Alexandrovitch gathered from her silence.

Alexey Alexandrovitch listened to her now, and the phrases that had earlier seemed to him, if not actually distasteful, at least overdone, now sounded natural and consoling. He had disliked this new enthusiastic strain of religion. He was a believer who was interested in religion mainly for its political aspect, and the new doctrine, which dared to offer several new interpretations — precisely because it opened the door to debate and analysis — was on principle disagreeable to him. He had until now taken a cold, even hostile, attitude toward this new teaching, and with Countess Lidia Ivanovna, who had been swept up by it, he had never argued, but had carefully fended off her attempts to draw him into argument by saying nothing. Now for the first time he listened to her words with pleasure, and inwardly did not push back against them.
"I am very, very grateful to you, both for what you have done and for what you have said," he said when she had finished praying.
Countess Lidia Ivanovna once more pressed both her friend's hands.
"Now I will start my duties," she said with a smile after a pause, as she wiped away the traces of tears. "I'm going to Seryozha. I'll only come to you as a last resort." And she got up and went out.
Countess Lidia Ivanovna went into Seryozha's part of the house and, letting tears fall on the frightened child's cheeks, told him that his father was a saint and his mother was dead.

Countess Lidia Ivanovna kept her promise. She really did take on the organization and running of Alexey Alexandrovitch's household. But she had not been exaggerating when she said practical matters were not her strong suit. Every arrangement she made had to be modified because it couldn't be carried out, and the modifications were made by Korney, Alexey Alexandrovitch's valet, who — without anyone realizing it — now actually ran Karenin's household and quietly, discreetly, reported to his master while dressing him on everything Karenin needed to know. But Lidia Ivanovna's help was real all the same: she gave Alexey Alexandrovitch moral support through her conscious love and respect for him, and — what was even more soothing for her to believe — she almost converted him to Christianity. That is, from an indifferent and listless believer she turned him into a fervent and committed adherent of the new interpretation of Christian doctrine that had lately been gaining ground in Petersburg. It was easy for Alexey Alexandrovitch to believe in this teaching. He, like Lidia Ivanovna and the others who shared their views, was entirely without vividness of imagination — that spiritual faculty by which the images called up by the imagination become so real that they have to be brought into line with other ideas and with actual facts. He saw nothing impossible or unthinkable in the idea that death, while it existed for unbelievers, did not exist for him; that since he possessed the most perfect faith — and he himself was the judge of how perfect it was — there was therefore no sin in his soul, and he was already experiencing complete salvation here on earth.

It is true that the falseness and shallowness of this conception of his faith were dimly available to Alexey Alexandrovitch himself, and he knew that back when he had given way to the feeling of forgiveness with no idea at all that his forgiveness was the act of a higher power, he had felt more happiness than he did now, when at every moment he was thinking that Christ was in his heart and that, in signing official papers, he was carrying out His will. But for Alexey Alexandrovitch it was a necessity to think in that way. It was such a necessity for him, in his humiliation, to have some elevated vantage point, however imaginary, from which — though he was looked down on by everyone — he could look down on others, that he clung, as to his sole salvation, to his illusion of salvation.

title: Chapter 23
paragraphs: Countess Lidia Ivanovna, as a very young and sentimental girl, had been married off to a wealthy man of high rank, an extremely good-natured, jovial, extremely dissipated rake. Two months after the wedding her husband left her, and met her impassioned declarations of love with sarcasm and even hostility — something that people who knew the count's good heart and saw no flaws in the sentimental Lidia could not explain. Though they were divorced and lived apart, the husband still treated her, whenever they happened to meet, with the same malicious irony, the source of which remained a mystery.

Countess Lidia Ivanovna had long since stopped being in love with her husband, but from that time on she had never stopped being in love with someone. She was in love with several people at once, men and women alike; she had been in love with almost anyone who had stood out in any way. She had been in love with all the new princes and princesses who married into the imperial family; she had been in love with a high Church dignitary, a vicar, and a parish priest; she had been in love with a journalist, three Slavophiles, with Komissarov, with a minister, a doctor, an English missionary, and with Karenin. All these passions, constantly waning or growing more intense, did not interfere with her keeping up an extensive and complicated set of relations at court and in fashionable society. But from the moment that, after Karenin's catastrophe, she took him under her particular protection — from the moment she started working in Karenin's household for his welfare — she felt that all her other attachments had not been the real thing, and that she was now genuinely in love, and only with Karenin. The feeling she had for him now seemed to her stronger than any of her earlier feelings. Analyzing her feeling and comparing it with previous passions, she clearly saw that she would not have been in love with Komissarov if he hadn't saved the life of the Tsar; that she would not have been in love with Ristitch-Kudzhitsky if there had been no Slavonic question; but that she loved Karenin for himself — for his lofty, misunderstood soul; for the high notes of his voice, which she found sweet; for his drawn-out way of speaking, his tired eyes, his character, and his soft white hands with their swollen veins. She was not merely thrilled when she met him; she scanned his face for signs of the impression she was making. She tried to please him not only with her words but with her whole self. For his sake she now took more care with her dress than before. She caught herself daydreaming about what might have been if she had not been married and he had been free. She blushed with emotion when he walked into the room; she couldn't hold back a smile of delight when he said anything kind to her.

For several days now Countess Lidia Ivanovna had been in a state of intense excitement. She had learned that Anna and Vronsky were in Petersburg. Alexey Alexandrovitch had to be saved from seeing her — even from the agonizing knowledge that that dreadful woman was in the same city and that he might run into her at any moment.

Lidia Ivanovna made inquiries through her friends about what those _infamous people_, as she called Anna and Vronsky, intended to do, and she did her best to steer her friend's movements during those days so that he could not cross paths with them. The young adjutant — an acquaintance of Vronsky's, through whom she got her information, and who was hoping to obtain a certain concession through Countess Lidia Ivanovna — told her that they had finished their business and were leaving the next day. Lidia Ivanovna had already begun to relax when, the next morning, a note was brought to her in handwriting she recognized with horror. It was Anna Karenina's handwriting. The envelope was made of paper as thick as tree bark; on the oblong yellow sheet there was a huge monogram, and the letter smelled of a pleasant perfume.
"Who brought it?"
"A messenger from the hotel."

It was some time before Countess Lidia Ivanovna could sit down to read the letter. Her excitement brought on an asthma attack, to which she was prone. When she had recovered her composure, she read the following letter, in French:
"Madame la Comtesse,

"The Christian feelings that fill your heart give me what I know to be unforgivable boldness in writing to you. I am wretched at being separated from my son. I beg permission to see him once before I leave. Forgive me for bringing myself back to your memory. I am writing to you and not to Alexey Alexandrovitch only because I do not wish to cause that generous man to suffer by remembering me. Knowing your friendship for him, I know you will understand me. Could you send Seryozha to me, or should I come to the house at some appointed hour, or will you let me know when and where I might see him somewhere else? I do not expect a refusal, knowing the magnanimity of the one in whose hands this rests. You cannot imagine how desperately I want to see him, and so you cannot imagine the gratitude your help would awaken in me.
"Anna."
Everything in this letter infuriated Countess Lidia Ivanovna: its content, the allusion to magnanimity, and especially what she considered its free-and-easy tone.
"Tell them there is no answer," said Countess Lidia Ivanovna, and immediately, opening her blotting book, she wrote to Alexey Alexandrovitch saying she hoped to see him at one o'clock at the levee.

"I have to talk with you about a grave and painful matter. We can arrange there where to meet. Best of all at my house, where I will order tea _the way you like it_. Urgent. He lays the cross, but He gives the strength to bear it," she added, to give him some hint of preparation. Countess Lidia Ivanovna usually wrote two or three letters a day to Alexey Alexandrovitch. She enjoyed that form of communication, which allowed for a refinement and air of mystery that their face-to-face meetings did not.

title: Chapter 24
paragraphs: The levee was winding down. People ran into one another on the way out and traded the latest gossip — the new honors just handed out and the changes among the higher-ups.

"If only Countess Marya Borissovna were Minister of War, and Princess Vatkovskaya Commander-in-Chief," said a gray-headed little old man in a gold-embroidered uniform, addressing a tall, handsome maid of honor who had asked him about the new appointments.
"And me as one of the adjutants," said the maid of honor, smiling.
"You have a post already. You're over the ecclesiastical department. And your assistant is Karenin."
"Good morning, prince!" said the little old man to a man who had come over to him.
"What were you saying about Karenin?" the prince asked.
"He and Putyatov have been given the Alexander Nevsky."
"I thought he already had it."

"No. Look at him over there," said the little old man, pointing with his embroidered hat at Karenin, in a court uniform with the new red ribbon across his shoulder, standing in the doorway of the hall with an influential member of the Imperial Council. "Happy as a kid with a penny," he added, breaking off to shake hands with a handsome, enormous gentleman of the bedchamber.
"No, he looks older," said the gentleman of the bedchamber.
"From overwork. He's always drawing up some new project. He won't let any poor devil go these days till he's gone through it with him point by point."
"Looking older, you say? _Il fait des passions_. I believe Countess Lidia Ivanovna is jealous of his wife now."
"Oh, come — please don't say anything bad about Countess Lidia Ivanovna."
"Why, what's bad about being in love with Karenin?"
"But is it true Madame Karenina is here?"
"Well, not here at the palace, but in Petersburg. I ran into her yesterday with Alexey Vronsky, _bras dessous, bras dessous_, on the Morskaya."
"_C'est un homme qui n'a pas_ ..." the gentleman of the bedchamber was beginning, but he broke off to bow and make way for a member of the imperial family to pass.

So people kept talking about Alexey Alexandrovitch, finding fault with him and laughing at him, while he, blocking the path of the member of the Imperial Council he had cornered, was walking him through his new financial project point by point, never pausing for an instant for fear the man would slip away.

Almost at the same time that his wife left him, Alexey Alexandrovitch had reached the bitterest moment in an official's life — the moment when his upward career stops dead. The stop had come, and everyone could see it, but Alexey Alexandrovitch himself was not yet aware that his career was over. Whether it was because of his feud with Stremov, or his misfortune with his wife, or simply that he had reached the limits set for him, it had become obvious to everyone in the course of that year that his career was finished. He still held an important post, sat on a number of commissions and committees, but he was a man whose day was done and from whom nothing more was expected. Whatever he said, whatever he proposed, was heard as if it were something everyone had known for ages and nobody needed. But Alexey Alexandrovitch had no inkling of this; on the contrary, now that he was cut off from any real share in the work of government, he saw more clearly than ever the errors and shortcomings in what others were doing, and felt it was his duty to point out how they could be corrected. Shortly after the separation from his wife, he began writing his first memorandum on the new judicial procedure — the first of an endless string of memoranda he was destined to produce.

Alexey Alexandrovitch not only failed to notice his hopeless standing in official Petersburg; not only was he free of any anxiety on that front; he was actually more satisfied with his own work than ever.

"He that is unmarried careth for the things that belong to the Lord, how he may please the Lord; but he that is married careth for the things that are of the world, how he may please his wife," says the Apostle Paul, and Alexey Alexandrovitch, who now took his guidance in every action from Scripture, often called this verse to mind. It seemed to him that ever since he had been left without a wife, he had been serving the Lord in these very reform projects more zealously than before.

The unmistakable impatience of the Council member trying to get away from him did not bother Alexey Alexandrovitch in the slightest; he only gave up his exposition when the Council member, seizing his chance as someone from the imperial family passed by, slipped off.
Left alone, Alexey Alexandrovitch looked down to collect his thoughts, then glanced around and walked toward the door, where he hoped to meet Countess Lidia Ivanovna.

"And how strong they all are, how physically sound," thought Alexey Alexandrovitch, looking at the powerfully built gentleman of the bedchamber with his well-combed, scented whiskers, and at the red neck of the prince pinched by his tight uniform. He had to pass them on his way. "Truly it is said that all the world is evil," he thought, with another sidelong glance at the calves of the gentleman of the bedchamber.

Moving forward at his deliberate pace, Alexey Alexandrovitch bowed with his usual air of weariness and dignity to the gentleman who had been talking about him, and, looking toward the door, his eyes searched for Countess Lidia Ivanovna.

"Ah, Alexey Alexandrovitch!" said the little old man, with a malicious gleam in his eye, just as Karenin drew level with them and was nodding with a cold gesture. "I haven't congratulated you yet," the old man went on, pointing to his newly received ribbon.
"Thank you," answered Alexey Alexandrovitch. "What an _exquisite_ day," he added, with his characteristic emphasis on the word _exquisite_.
He was well aware they were laughing at him, but he didn't expect anything from them but hostility; he was used to it by now.

Catching sight of Lidia Ivanovna's yellow shoulders sticking up above her corset, and her fine pensive eyes summoning him over, Alexey Alexandrovitch smiled, showing his still-white teeth, and went toward her.

Lidia Ivanovna's dress had cost her great effort, as had every dress of hers lately. Her aim in dress now was the exact opposite of what it had been thirty years before. Back then she had wanted to adorn herself with everything she could, the more the better. Now, on the contrary, she was forced to be decked out in ways so out of keeping with her age and her figure that her sole concern was to make sure the contrast between the adornments and her own appearance was not too ghastly. And as far as Alexey Alexandrovitch was concerned she succeeded, and in his eyes she was attractive. For him she was the one island — not just of goodwill, but of love — in the sea of hostility and mockery around him.
Walking through rows of ironic eyes, he was drawn to her loving gaze as naturally as a plant to the sun.
"I congratulate you," she said, her eyes on his ribbon.

Suppressing a smile of pleasure, he shrugged and closed his eyes, as if to say that something like this could not be a source of joy to him. Countess Lidia Ivanovna knew perfectly well that it was in fact one of his greatest satisfactions, though he would never admit it.
"How is our angel?" said Countess Lidia Ivanovna, meaning Seryozha.

"I can't say I was entirely pleased with him," said Alexey Alexandrovitch, raising his eyebrows and opening his eyes. "And Sitnikov isn't satisfied with him either." (Sitnikov was the tutor in charge of Seryozha's secular education.) "As I've mentioned to you, there's a sort of coldness in him toward precisely the questions that ought to touch the heart of every man and every child...." Alexey Alexandrovitch launched into his views on the one subject besides the service that interested him — the education of his son.

Once Alexey Alexandrovitch, with Lidia Ivanovna's help, had been brought back to life and activity, he felt it was his duty to take charge of the education of the son left on his hands. Having never before shown any interest in educational questions, he devoted some time to studying the subject theoretically. After reading several books on anthropology, education, and didactics, he drew up a plan of study, hired the best tutor in Petersburg to supervise it, and got to work, and the subject went on absorbing him.
"Yes, but the heart. I see his father's heart in him, and with such a heart a child cannot go far wrong," said Lidia Ivanovna with enthusiasm.
"Yes, perhaps.... As for me, I do my duty. That is all I can do."

"You're coming to me," Countess Lidia Ivanovna said after a pause. "We have to discuss something that's painful for you. I would have given anything to spare you certain memories, but others don't see it that way. I've received a letter from _her_. _She_ is here in Petersburg."
Alexey Alexandrovitch shuddered at the reference to his wife, but his face immediately took on that corpse-like stiffness that expressed his complete helplessness in the matter.
"I was expecting it," he said.
Countess Lidia Ivanovna gazed at him in rapture, and tears of admiration at the greatness of his soul came into her eyes.

title: Chapter 25
paragraphs: When Alexey Alexandrovitch came into Countess Lidia Ivanovna's snug little boudoir, decorated with old china and hung with portraits, the lady herself had not yet appeared.
She was changing.

A cloth had been laid on a round table, and on it stood a china tea service and a silver spirit lamp and tea kettle. Alexey Alexandrovitch looked absently around at the endless familiar portraits decorating the room, sat down at the table, and opened a New Testament lying there. The rustle of the countess's silk skirt drew his attention away.
"Well, now we can sit quietly," said Countess Lidia Ivanovna, slipping with an agitated smile between the table and the sofa, "and talk over our tea."
After a few preparatory remarks, Countess Lidia Ivanovna, breathing hard and turning crimson, put the letter she had received into Alexey Alexandrovitch's hands.
After reading the letter, he sat for a long time in silence.
"I don't think I have the right to refuse her," he said, raising his eyes timidly.
"Dear friend, you never see evil in anyone!"
"On the contrary, I see that everything is evil. But whether it's just...."
His face showed indecision and a search for counsel, support, and guidance in a matter he didn't understand.

"No," Countess Lidia Ivanovna cut him off. "There are limits to everything. I can understand immorality," she said, not quite truthfully, since she had never been able to understand what leads women to immorality, "but I cannot understand cruelty. To whom? To you! How can she stay in the same town as you? No, the longer one lives, the more one learns. And I am learning to see your loftiness and her baseness."

"Who is to throw a stone?" said Alexey Alexandrovitch, clearly pleased with the part he had to play. "I have forgiven everything, and so I cannot deny her what her love calls for — her love for her son...."

"But is it love, my friend? Is it sincere? Granted, you have forgiven, you do forgive — do we have the right to play on the feelings of that angel? He thinks she is dead. He prays for her, and asks God to have mercy on her sins. And it is better that way. But now what will he think?"
"I had not thought of that," said Alexey Alexandrovitch, evidently agreeing.
Countess Lidia Ivanovna covered her face with her hands and was silent. She was praying.

"If you ask my advice," she said, lifting her face once she had finished her prayer, "I do not advise it. Do you think I can't see how you are suffering, how this has reopened your wounds? But say that, as always, you put yourself aside — what can come of it? More suffering for you, and torment for the child. If there were a trace of humanity left in her, she ought not to want this herself. No, I have no hesitation in saying I advise against it, and if you'll entrust it to me, I will write to her."
And Alexey Alexandrovitch agreed, and Countess Lidia Ivanovna sent the following letter, in French:
"Dear Madame,

"Reminding your son of you might lead to questions on his part which could not be answered without planting in the child's soul a spirit of criticism toward what ought to be sacred to him, and therefore I beg you to take your husband's refusal in the spirit of Christian love. I pray to Almighty God to have mercy on you.
"Countess Lidia."
This letter achieved the hidden purpose Countess Lidia Ivanovna had concealed even from herself. It cut Anna to the quick.

For his part, Alexey Alexandrovitch, on returning home from Lidia Ivanovna's, could not for the rest of the day settle to his usual occupations or recover the spiritual peace of a man saved and believing that he had lately been feeling.

The thought of his wife, who had sinned so badly against him, and toward whom he had behaved so saintly (as Countess Lidia Ivanovna had rightly told him), should not have troubled him; but it did. He could not concentrate on the book he was reading; he could not push away nagging memories of his dealings with her, of the mistake — as it now looked — he had made about her. The memory of how he had received her confession of infidelity on the way home from the races (especially that he had insisted only on the keeping up of outward appearances and had not sent a challenge) tortured him like remorse. He was also tormented by the thought of the letter he had written her; and most of all his forgiveness, which nobody had wanted, and his care for another man's child made his heart burn with shame and remorse.
And he felt that same shame and regret now, as he reviewed all of his past with her, recalling the awkward words in which, after long hesitation, he had proposed.

"But how am I to blame?" he asked himself. And that question always stirred up another in him — whether they did things differently, did their loving and marrying differently, these Vronskys and Oblonskys ... these gentlemen of the bedchamber with their fine calves. A whole parade of such spirited, vigorous, self-confident men passed through his mind, men who always and everywhere drew his curious attention against his will. He tried to push these thoughts away, tried to persuade himself that he was not living for this passing life but for the life of eternity, and that there was peace and love in his heart.

But the fact that in this passing, trivial life he had — as it seemed to him — made a few trivial mistakes tortured him as though the eternal salvation he believed in did not exist. But the temptation did not last long, and soon the peace and elevation by virtue of which he could forget what he did not want to remember was reestablished once again in Alexey Alexandrovitch's soul.

title: Chapter 26
paragraphs: "Well, Kapitonitch?" said Seryozha, coming back rosy and cheerful from his walk the day before his birthday and handing his overcoat to the tall old hall-porter, who smiled down at the little fellow from the height of his long frame. "Well, has the bandaged clerk been here today? Did papa see him?"
"He saw him. The moment the chief secretary came out, I announced him," said the hall-porter with a good-humored wink. "Here, I'll take it off."

"Seryozha!" called the tutor, stopping in the doorway to the inner rooms. "Take it off yourself." But Seryozha, though he heard the tutor's reedy voice, paid no attention. He stayed there holding on to the hall-porter's belt and staring up into his face.
"Well, and did papa do what he wanted for him?"

The hall-porter nodded yes. The clerk with the bandaged face, who had come seven times already to ask some favor of Alexey Alexandrovitch, was a person of interest to both Seryozha and the hall-porter. Seryozha had come across him in the hall and had overheard him pleading with the hall-porter to announce him, saying that he and his children had death staring them in the face.
Since then, after running into him again in the hall, Seryozha had taken a real interest in him.
"Well, was he very glad?" he asked.
"Glad? I should think so! Practically dancing on the way out."
"And has anything been brought?" Seryozha asked after a pause.
"Come now, sir," said the hall-porter; then, with a shake of his head, he whispered, "Something from the countess."
Seryozha understood at once that the hall-porter meant a present from Countess Lidia Ivanovna for his birthday.
"What? Where?"
"Korney took it up to your papa. Must be a fine toy too!"
"How big? Like this?"
"On the small side, but a fine thing."
"A book."

"No, a thing. Off you go, off you go, Vassily Lukitch is calling for you," said the porter, hearing the tutor's steps coming closer, and carefully prying the little hand in the half-pulled-off glove from his belt, he nodded toward the tutor.
"Vassily Lukitch, in just a tiny minute!" answered Seryozha with that cheerful, affectionate smile that always won over the conscientious Vassily Lukitch.

Seryozha was too happy, the whole day was too delightful, for him not to share with his friend the porter the family good news he had heard during his walk in the public gardens from Lidia Ivanovna's niece. This piece of news struck him as especially important because it had come at the same time as the bandaged clerk's happiness and his own at having had toys delivered for him. It seemed to Seryozha that this was a day on which everyone ought to be cheerful and happy.
"You know papa was given the Alexander Nevsky today?"
"Of course I know! People have already been by to congratulate him."
"And is he glad?"
"Glad at the Tsar's gracious favor! I should think so! It's proof he's deserved it," said the porter, severe and serious.

Seryozha drifted into a daydream, staring up at the porter's face, which he had studied thoroughly down to every detail — especially the chin hanging between the gray whiskers, a part of him no one ever saw except Seryozha, who only ever looked at him from below.
"Well, and has your daughter been to see you lately?"
The porter's daughter was a ballet dancer.
"When is she supposed to come on weekdays? They've got their lessons to learn too. And you have your lesson, sir. Off you go."
When Seryozha came into the room, instead of sitting down to his lessons he told his tutor about his theory that what had been brought for him must be a machine. "What do you think?" he asked.
But Vassily Lukitch was thinking only about the grammar lesson that had to be learned for the teacher who was coming at two.

"No, just tell me, Vassily Lukitch," he asked suddenly, once he was seated at the work table with his book in his hands, "what is greater than the Alexander Nevsky? You know papa was given the Alexander Nevsky?"
Vassily Lukitch replied that the Vladimir was greater than the Alexander Nevsky.
"And higher still?"
"Well, highest of all is the Andrey Pervozvanny."
"And higher than the Andrey?"
"I don't know."
"What, you don't know?" And Seryozha, resting on his elbows, sank into deep thought.

His thoughts were of the most complicated and varied kind. He imagined his father suddenly being awarded both the Vladimir and the Andrey today, and as a result being much friendlier at the lesson; and he daydreamed about how, when he was grown up, he would win all the orders himself, and what they might invent that was higher than the Andrey. As soon as any higher order was invented, he would win it. They would make a higher one still, and he would immediately win that one too.

Time passed in this daydreaming, and when the teacher arrived the lesson on adverbs of place, time, and manner of action was not ready, and the teacher was not just displeased but actually hurt. That got to Seryozha. He felt he was not to blame for not having learned it; no matter how he tried, he simply could not do it. While the teacher was explaining it to him, he believed him and seemed to follow, but the moment he was left on his own, he genuinely could not remember or understand that the short, familiar word "suddenly" is an adverb of manner of action. Still, he was sorry to have let the teacher down.
He picked a moment when the teacher was looking silently at the book.
"Mihail Ivanitch, when is your birthday?" he asked all of a sudden.
"You'd do better to be thinking about your work. Birthdays mean nothing to a rational being. It's a day like any other on which one has to do one's work."

Seryozha gazed intently at the teacher — at his thin beard, at his spectacles, which had slid down past the bump on his nose — and fell into such a deep reverie that he heard nothing of what the teacher was explaining. He knew the teacher didn't believe what he was saying; he could tell from the tone in which it was said. "But why have they all agreed to say nothing but the dreariest, most useless things, all the time? Why does he keep me at arm's length? Why doesn't he love me?" he asked himself sadly, and could find no answer.

title: Chapter 27
paragraphs: After the grammar teacher's lesson came his father's lesson. While he waited for his father, Seryozha sat at the table playing with a penknife and slipped into a daydream. One of his favorite things to do was to look for his mother on his walks. He didn't really believe in death in general, and certainly not in her death — in spite of what Lidia Ivanovna had told him and his father had confirmed — and it was precisely because of that, and after they had told him she was dead, that he had started looking for her whenever he went out. Every woman with a full, graceful figure and dark hair was his mother. At the sight of such a woman, such a wave of tenderness rose in him that his breath caught and tears came to his eyes. And he was on tiptoe with expectation that she would walk up to him, lift her veil — and her whole face would be visible, she would smile, she would hug him, he would catch her scent, feel the softness of her arms, and cry with happiness, just the way he had one evening lying in her lap while she tickled him, and he laughed and bit her white fingers covered with rings. Later, when he found out by accident from his old nurse that his mother was not dead, and his father and Lidia Ivanovna had explained to him that she was dead to him because she was wicked (which he simply could not believe, because he loved her), he went on looking and waiting for her in the same way. That day in the public gardens there had been a lady in a lilac veil whom he had watched with a pounding heart, sure it was her as she came toward them along the path. The lady hadn't come up to them — she had vanished somewhere. That day, more intensely than ever, Seryozha felt a rush of love for her, and now, waiting for his father, he forgot everything else and cut all the way around the edge of the table with his penknife, staring straight ahead with shining eyes and daydreaming about her.
"Here's your papa!" said Vassily Lukitch, snapping him out of it.
Seryozha jumped up and went over to his father, kissed his hand, and looked at him intently, trying to spot signs of pleasure at the Alexander Nevsky.

"Did you have a nice walk?" said Alexey Alexandrovitch, settling into his easy chair, pulling the volume of the Old Testament toward him, and opening it. Although Alexey Alexandrovitch had told Seryozha more than once that every Christian should know Bible history thoroughly, he often consulted the Bible himself during the lesson, and Seryozha noticed it.

"Yes, it was very nice, papa," said Seryozha, sitting sideways on his chair and rocking it, which was against the rules. "I saw Nadinka" (Nadinka was a niece of Lidia Ivanovna's who was being brought up in her house). "She told me you'd been given a new star. Are you glad, papa?"

"First of all, please don't rock your chair," said Alexey Alexandrovitch. "And secondly, it isn't the reward that matters, but the work itself. I wish you'd understand that. If you take up your work, your studies, in order to win a reward, the work will seem hard to you; but when you work" — and Alexey Alexandrovitch, as he spoke, thought about how sense of duty had carried him through the dreary labor of the morning, which had consisted of signing one hundred and eighty papers — "loving your work, you will find your reward in the work itself."

Seryozha's eyes, which had been bright with cheerfulness and affection, went dull and dropped before his father's gaze. This was the same long-familiar tone his father always took with him, and Seryozha had learned by now to fall in with it. His father always talked to him — so Seryozha felt — as if he were addressing some imaginary boy, one of those boys who exist in books and are nothing like himself. So with his father Seryozha always tried to play the part of the storybook boy.
"You understand that, I hope?" said his father.
"Yes, papa," answered Seryozha, playing the imaginary boy.

The lesson was to learn by heart several verses from the Gospel and to recite the opening of the Old Testament. The verses from the Gospel Seryozha knew fairly well, but at the moment he was saying them he became so absorbed in watching the sharp, bony ridge of his father's forehead that he lost the thread, and he muddled the end of one verse with the beginning of another. So Alexey Alexandrovitch could tell he didn't understand what he was saying, and that irritated him.

He frowned and began explaining something Seryozha had heard many times and could never remember, because he understood it far too well — the same way that "suddenly" is an adverb of manner of action. Seryozha looked at his father with frightened eyes and could think only of whether his father would make him repeat what had just been said, as he sometimes did. And the thought so alarmed Seryozha that he now understood nothing at all. But his father did not make him repeat it, and moved on to the lesson from the Old Testament. Seryozha recounted the events themselves well enough, but when he was asked what certain events prefigured, he knew nothing, even though he had already been punished over this particular lesson. The passage at which he could not say a word, and started fidgeting and slicing at the table and rocking his chair, was where he was supposed to recite the patriarchs before the Flood. He didn't know a single one of them except Enoch, who had been taken up alive into heaven. Last time he had remembered their names, but now he had forgotten them completely — mainly because Enoch was his favorite person in the whole Old Testament, and Enoch being carried up to heaven was tied in his head to a long chain of thought, and he sank into that thought now while he stared, transfixed, at his father's watch-chain and a half-undone button on his waistcoat.

Seryozha utterly disbelieved in death, which they talked to him about so often. He didn't believe the people he loved could die, and above all that he himself would die. That was something completely unthinkable, impossible for him. But he had been told that everyone dies; he had even asked people he trusted, and they had confirmed it; his old nurse had said the same, though unwillingly. But Enoch hadn't died, so it followed that not everyone died. "And why can't someone else serve God like that and be taken up alive into heaven?" thought Seryozha. Bad people — meaning people Seryozha didn't like — they could die, but the good ones might all be like Enoch.
"Well, what are the names of the patriarchs?"
"Enoch, Enos —"

"You've said that already. This is bad, Seryozha, very bad. If you don't try to learn what is more necessary than anything for a Christian," said his father, getting up, "whatever can interest you? I am displeased with you, and Piotr Ignatitch" (this was the most important of his teachers) "is displeased with you.... I shall have to punish you."

His father and his teacher were both displeased with Seryozha, and he really did learn his lessons very badly. But he was not a stupid boy. On the contrary, he was far cleverer than the boys his teacher held up to him as examples. In his father's opinion, he didn't want to learn what he was being taught. In reality he couldn't learn it. He couldn't, because the claims of his own soul were more compelling to him than the claims his father and his teacher made on him. The two sets of claims were in conflict, and he was in direct opposition to his education. He was nine years old; he was a child; but he knew his own soul, it was precious to him, he guarded it the way the eyelid guards the eye, and without the key of love he let no one inside it. His teachers complained that he wouldn't learn, while his soul was brimming over with thirst for knowledge. And he was learning — from Kapitonitch, from his nurse, from Nadinka, from Vassily Lukitch — just not from his teachers. The stream his father and his teachers were counting on to turn their mill-wheels had long since dried up at the source, but its waters were doing their work in a different channel.

His father punished Seryozha by not letting him go visit Nadinka, Lidia Ivanovna's niece; but the punishment turned out happily for Seryozha. Vassily Lukitch was in a good mood and showed him how to make windmills. The whole evening went by on this project, and on dreaming about how to build a windmill he could ride on himself — grabbing onto the sails or strapping himself in and spinning round. Seryozha did not think about his mother all evening, but once he was in bed he suddenly remembered her, and in his own words he prayed that his mother, for his birthday tomorrow, would stop hiding herself and come to him.
"Vassily Lukitch, do you know what extra thing I prayed for tonight, besides the usual?"
"That you'd learn your lessons better?"
"No."
"Toys?"
"No. You'll never guess. A splendid thing — but it's a secret! When it happens, I'll tell you. Can't you guess?"
"No, I can't guess. Tell me yourself," said Vassily Lukitch with a smile, which was rare with him. "Come on, lie down, I'm putting out the candle."
"Without the candle I can see better what I see and what I prayed for. There — I almost gave away the secret!" said Seryozha, laughing happily.

When the candle was taken away, Seryozha heard and felt his mother. She was standing over him, caressing him with loving eyes. But then came windmills, a knife, everything began to mix together, and he fell asleep.

title: Chapter 28
paragraphs: When they arrived in Petersburg, Vronsky and Anna took rooms at one of the best hotels. Vronsky stayed on a lower floor, while Anna had a large suite of four rooms upstairs with the baby, the nurse, and her maid.

On the day of his arrival Vronsky called on his brother. He found his mother there, in from Moscow on business. His mother and sister-in-law received him as they always did. They asked about his time abroad and chatted about the people they all knew, but neither said a single word about his connection with Anna. His brother came round the next morning to see Vronsky and, on his own, asked about her. Alexey Vronsky told him plainly that he considered his connection with Madame Karenina a marriage, that he hoped to arrange a divorce and then to marry her, and that until then he regarded her as much his wife as anyone else's. He asked his brother to tell their mother and his sister-in-law the same.
"If society disapproves, I don't care," Vronsky said. "But if my family wants to keep up family ties with me, they'll have to keep them up with my wife on the same footing."

The elder brother, who had always respected the younger one's judgment, couldn't really say whether Alexey was right or not until the world had ruled on it. As far as he himself was concerned, he had no objection, and together with Alexey he went up to see Anna.

In front of his brother, as in front of everyone else, Vronsky addressed Anna with a certain formality, treating her like a very close friend. But it was understood that his brother knew what was really between them, and they talked about Anna going down to Vronsky's country estate.

For all his experience in society, Vronsky was, because of the new position he was in, laboring under a strange illusion. You would have thought he'd have grasped that society was now closed to him and Anna, but instead vague notions had floated up in his head that this was only the case in the old days, and that now, with the speed of modern progress (he had become, without noticing, a partisan of every variety of progress), society's views had shifted, and whether they would be received in society was not a foregone conclusion. "Of course," he thought, "she won't be received at court, but our close friends can and must take the right view of it." You can sit for hours on end with your legs crossed in the same position if you know nothing prevents you from changing it. But if a man knows he has to sit that way with his legs crossed, then the cramps set in, the legs start twitching and pulling toward wherever he'd like to move them. That was what Vronsky was going through with respect to society. At the bottom of his heart he knew the world was shut against them, but he was testing whether the world might not have changed by now and might receive them after all. He soon saw, though, that while society was open to him personally, it was closed to Anna. As in the game of cat and mouse, the hands raised to let him through dropped to bar Anna's way.
One of the first ladies of Petersburg society Vronsky saw was his cousin Betsy.

"At last!" she greeted him happily. "And Anna? How glad I am! Where are you staying? I can imagine that after your wonderful travels you must find our poor Petersburg dreadful. I can just picture your honeymoon in Rome. What about the divorce? Is that all settled?"
Vronsky noticed that Betsy's enthusiasm cooled when she learned no divorce had been granted yet.
"People will throw stones at me, I know," she said, "but I'll come and see Anna. Yes, I'll definitely come. You won't be here long, I take it?"

And she did indeed come to see Anna that same day, but her tone was nothing like the old one. She was visibly proud of her own courage and wanted Anna to appreciate the loyalty of her friendship. She stayed only ten minutes, talked about society gossip, and as she was leaving said:

"You've never told me when the divorce is to be? Suppose I'm ready to throw my cap over the windmill — other stiff-necked people will give you the cold shoulder until you're married. And these days it's so simple. _Ça se fait_. So you're leaving Friday? A pity we shan't see each other again."

From Betsy's tone Vronsky could have grasped what he had to expect from the world, but he made another attempt within his own family. He didn't count on his mother. He knew that his mother, who had been so excited about Anna when they first met, would have no mercy on her now for having ruined her son's career. He had more hope of Varya, his brother's wife. He imagined she wouldn't throw stones, that she would go straight and simply to see Anna and receive her in her own house.
The day after his arrival Vronsky went to her, and finding her alone, told her directly what he wanted.

"You know, Alexey," she said after hearing him out, "how fond I am of you, and how ready I am to do anything for you. But I haven't spoken up, because I knew I couldn't be of any use to you or to Anna Arkadyevna," she said, articulating the name "Anna Arkadyevna" with particular care. "Please don't think I'm judging her. Never. In her place I might have done the same. I don't, I can't go into that," she said, glancing nervously at his dark face. "But one has to call things by their names. You want me to go and see her, to invite her here, and to bring her back into society — but please understand that _I cannot_ do that. I have daughters growing up, and I have to live in society for my husband's sake. Look, I'm willing to go and see Anna Arkadyevna. She'll understand that I can't invite her here — or I'd have to invite her in such a way that she wouldn't meet people who see things differently, and that would offend her. I can't lift her back up.…"
"Oh, I don't see her as any more fallen than the hundreds of women you do receive!" Vronsky cut in, gloomier still, and got up in silence, realizing that his sister-in-law's mind was made up.
"Alexey! Don't be angry with me. Please understand that it's not my fault," Varya began, looking at him with a timid smile.

"I'm not angry with you," he said, still grim. "But it grieves me on two counts. It also grieves me that this means our friendship has to break — or if not break, at least cool. You can see that for me too it can't be any other way."
And with that he left her.

Vronsky knew that further effort was pointless, that he would have to get through these few days in Petersburg as if he were in a strange town — avoiding any contact with his old circle so as not to be exposed to the slights and humiliations he found so unbearable. One of the most unpleasant features of his situation in Petersburg was that Alexey Alexandrovitch and his name seemed to meet him everywhere. He couldn't start talking about anything without the conversation veering toward Alexey Alexandrovitch; he couldn't go anywhere without the risk of running into him. So at least it felt to Vronsky — the way it feels to a man with a sore finger that he keeps catching it on every object, as if on purpose.

Their stay in Petersburg was all the more painful to Vronsky because he was aware, the whole time, of some new mood in Anna that he couldn't make out. At one moment she would seem in love with him, and the next she would turn cold, irritable, and unreadable. She was worrying about something, holding something back from him, and didn't seem to register the humiliations that were poisoning his life — humiliations that, given her fine intuition, must have been even more unbearable for her.

title: Chapter 29
paragraphs: One of Anna's reasons for coming back to Russia had been to see her son. From the day she'd left Italy the thought of it had never stopped agitating her. The closer she got to Petersburg, the greater the joy and importance of the meeting grew in her imagination. She didn't even ask herself how to arrange it. It seemed natural and simple to her — she would see her son once she was in the same city as him. But on arriving in Petersburg she was suddenly made sharply aware of her present position in society, and grasped that arranging this meeting was no easy matter.

She had been in Petersburg for two days now. The thought of her son hadn't left her for a moment, but she hadn't yet seen him. Going straight to the house, where she might run into Alexey Alexandrovitch — that, she felt, she had no right to do. She might be turned away and insulted. Writing to him, and so opening up some kind of relationship with her husband — that was misery just to think about; she could only be at peace when she didn't think of her husband at all. Catching a glimpse of her son out walking — finding out where and when he went out — wasn't enough; she had looked forward to this meeting so much, she had so much to say to him, she so longed to hold him and kiss him. Seryozha's old nurse might be able to help and tell her what to do. But the nurse no longer lived at Alexey Alexandrovitch's house. In all this uncertainty, and in trying to track down the nurse, two days had slipped past.

Having heard about the close friendship between Alexey Alexandrovitch and Countess Lidia Ivanovna, Anna decided on the third day to write the countess a letter, which cost her great effort, and in which she said pointedly that permission to see her son must rest on her husband's generosity. She knew that if the letter were shown to her husband, he would keep up his pose of magnanimity and would not refuse her request.

The messenger who took the letter brought back the most cruel, unexpected answer: there was no answer. She had never felt so humiliated as the moment when, summoning the messenger, she heard from him the exact account of how he had waited, and how he had then been told there was no answer. Anna felt humiliated, insulted, but she saw that from her own point of view Countess Lidia Ivanovna was in the right. Her pain was sharper because she had to bear it alone. She couldn't and wouldn't share it with Vronsky. She knew that to him — though he was the original cause of her distress — the question of seeing her son would seem trivial. She knew that he would never be capable of understanding the depth of her suffering, that his cool tone at the slightest mention of it would make her start to hate him. And she dreaded that more than anything in the world, so she hid from him everything to do with her son. She spent the entire day at home, turning over ways of seeing him, and had decided to write to her husband. She was actually composing the letter when Lidia Ivanovna's reply was handed to her. The countess's silence had subdued and depressed her, but the letter — everything she read between its lines — so infuriated her, this malice was so revolting set against her passionate, lawful tenderness for her son, that she turned against everyone else and stopped blaming herself.

"This coldness — this performance of feeling!" she said to herself. "They have to insult me and torture the child, and I'm supposed to put up with it! Under no circumstances! She's worse than I am. At least I don't lie." And on the spot she decided that the next day, Seryozha's birthday, she would go straight to her husband's house, bribe or trick the servants — whatever it took — see her son, and overturn the hideous fiction they were wrapping the unhappy child in.

She went to a toy shop, bought toys, and thought through her plan. She would go early in the morning at eight o'clock, when Alexey Alexandrovitch was sure not to be up. She'd have money ready to give the hall-porter and the footman so they would let her in. Without lifting her veil, she would say she'd come from Seryozha's godfather to wish him a happy birthday and had been asked to leave the toys by his bedside. She had worked out everything except the words she would say to her son. As often as she'd dreamed of it, she still couldn't think of anything to say.
The next morning at eight, Anna got out of a hired sledge and rang at the front door of her former home.

"Go and see what they want. Some lady," said Kapitonitch — who, not yet dressed, in his overcoat and galoshes, had peeped out of the window and spotted a veiled lady standing right at the door. His assistant, a boy Anna didn't know, had hardly opened the door for her before she stepped inside and quickly pressed a three-rouble note from her muff into his hand.
"Seryozha — Sergey Alexeitch," she said, and was about to walk on. Studying the note, the porter's assistant stopped her at the second glass door.
"Who do you want to see?" he asked.
She didn't take in his words and gave no answer.
Noticing the strange lady's confusion, Kapitonitch came over to her, opened the second door for her, and asked what she would like.
"From Prince Skorodumov for Sergey Alexeitch," she said.
"He's not up yet," said the porter, looking at her closely.

Anna hadn't expected that the entirely unchanged front hall of the house where she had lived for nine years would affect her so much. Memories, sweet and painful, rose up one after another in her heart, and for a moment she forgot what she was there for.
"Would you mind waiting?" said Kapitonitch, taking off her fur cloak.
As he removed the cloak, Kapitonitch glanced at her face, recognized her, and made her a low, silent bow.
"Please come in, your excellency," he said.

She tried to say something, but no sound would come; with a guilty, pleading glance at the old man she went up the stairs with light, swift steps. Bent over, his galoshes catching on the steps, Kapitonitch ran after her, trying to keep up.
"The tutor's in there. He may not be dressed. I'll let him know."
Anna kept climbing the familiar staircase, not taking in what the old man was saying.

"This way, to the left, if you please. Excuse the state of it. His honor's in the old parlor now," the hall-porter said, out of breath. "Excuse me, wait just a moment, your excellency. I'll go and check," he said, and overtaking her, opened the high door and disappeared behind it. Anna stood waiting. "He's only just woken up," the hall-porter said as he came back out. And at the very moment the porter said this, Anna caught the sound of a child's yawn. From the sound of that yawn alone she recognized her son and seemed to see him alive in front of her.

"Let me in. Go away!" she said, and walked in through the high doorway. To the right of the door stood a bed, and the boy was sitting up in it. His little body bent forward, his nightshirt unbuttoned, he was stretching and still yawning. The instant his lips came together they curled into a blissful, sleepy smile, and with that smile he slowly and deliciously rolled back again.
"Seryozha!" she whispered, going noiselessly up to him.

While they had been apart, and all through the recent weeks when she'd been feeling a fresh surge of love for him, she had pictured him as he had been at four — the age she had loved him most. Now he wasn't even what he'd been when she left him; he was further still from the four-year-old, taller and thinner. How thin his face was, how short his hair was cut! What long hands! How he'd changed since she left him! But it was still him — his head, his lips, his soft neck, his broad little shoulders.
"Seryozha!" she said again, right by the child's ear.

He propped himself up on his elbow again, turned his tangled head from side to side as if searching for something, and opened his eyes. Slowly, questioningly, he looked for a few seconds at his mother standing motionless before him, and then all at once he broke into a blissful smile, and shutting his eyes, rolled — not back, but toward her, into her arms.

"Seryozha! My darling boy!" she said, breathing hard and wrapping her arms around his plump little body. "Mother!" he said, wriggling about in her arms so as to touch her hands with every part of him at once.

Still smiling sleepily with his eyes closed, he flung his fat little arms around her shoulders, rolled toward her with the delicious sleepy warmth and smell only children have, and started rubbing his face against her neck and shoulders.
"I know," he said, opening his eyes. "It's my birthday today. I knew you'd come. I'll get up in a minute."
And with that he fell asleep.

Anna looked at him hungrily; she saw how he had grown and changed in her absence. She both knew and didn't know those bare legs, so long now, sticking out from under the quilt — those short-cropped curls on his neck where she had kissed him so often. She touched all of this and could say nothing; tears were choking her.
"What are you crying about, mother?" he said, waking up fully. "Mother, what are you crying about?" he called in a tearful voice.

"I won't cry.… I'm crying for joy. It's been so long since I've seen you. I won't, I won't," she said, swallowing back the tears and turning her face away. "Come on, it's time for you to get dressed," she added after a moment, and, never letting go of his hands, sat down on the chair by his bed where his clothes had been laid out.
"How do you get dressed without me? How…?" She tried to start chatting simply and brightly, but she couldn't, and again she had to turn away.
"I don't take cold baths. Papa didn't order them. And have you not seen Vassily Lukitch yet? He'll be in soon. Look — you're sitting on my clothes!"
And Seryozha burst into a peal of laughter. She looked at him and smiled.
"Mother, darling, sweet one!" he cried, throwing himself on her again and hugging her. It was as if only now, seeing her smile, did he fully realize what had happened.
"I don't want that on you," he said, lifting off her hat. And as though seeing her freshly without it, he fell to kissing her all over again.
"But what did you think about me? You didn't think I was dead?"
"I never believed it."
"You didn't believe it, sweetheart?"
"I knew, I knew!" he repeated, his favorite phrase, and snatching the hand that was stroking his hair, he pressed the open palm to his mouth and kissed it.

title: Chapter 30
paragraphs: Meanwhile Vassily Lukitch hadn't at first realized who the lady was, and gathered from their conversation that she was none other than the mother who had left her husband — whom he had never seen, since he had taken the post after her departure. He hesitated about whether to go in, or to send word to Alexey Alexandrovitch. Reflecting in the end that his duty was to get Seryozha up at the appointed hour, and that it was not his business to consider who was in the room — mother or anyone else — but simply to do his job, he finished dressing, went to the door, and opened it.
But the mother's and child's embraces, the sound of their voices, and what they were saying, made him change his mind.
He shook his head, sighed, and closed the door again. "I'll give it another ten minutes," he said to himself, clearing his throat and wiping his eyes.

Among the household servants there was intense excitement all this while. Everyone had heard that their mistress was back, that Kapitonitch had let her in, and that she was at that very moment in the nursery. They all knew the master always went in person to the nursery at nine, and they all understood perfectly that the husband and wife could not be allowed to meet, and that they must prevent it. Korney, the valet, went down to the porter's room, asked who had let her in and how it had happened, and on learning that Kapitonitch had admitted her and shown her up, gave the old man a piece of his mind. The hall-porter was stubbornly silent, but when Korney told him he ought to be sacked, Kapitonitch shot up to him, waved his hands in Korney's face, and started:

"Oh yes, of course you wouldn't have let her in! After ten years' service, never a hard word from her, and now you'd come out with, 'Off with you, get out, get going!' Oh yes, you're a sharp one at politics, no doubt! You don't need to be taught how to swindle the master and lift fur coats!"

"Soldier!" Korney said with contempt, and turned to the nurse, who was just coming in. "Here, what do you make of this, Marya Efimovna — he let her in without a word to anyone," Korney said to her. "Alexey Alexandrovitch will be down any minute now — and he'll go straight into the nursery!"
"A fine business, a fine business!" said the nurse. "You'd best find some way to delay him, Korney Vassilievitch — keep the master back — while I go and get her out somehow. A fine business!"

When the nurse came into the nursery, Seryozha was telling his mother how he and Nadinka had taken a tumble going downhill in the sledge and had turned over three times. She was listening to the sound of his voice, watching his face and the play of expression on it, holding his hand, but she wasn't following what he was saying. She had to go, she had to leave him — that was the only thing she was thinking and feeling. She heard Vassily Lukitch's footsteps come up to the door, then his cough; she heard the nurse's footsteps approaching too. But she sat as if turned to stone, unable to begin speaking or to get up.
"Mistress, darling!" the nurse began, going up to Anna and kissing her hands and shoulders. "God's brought joy to our boy on his birthday after all. You haven't changed one bit."
"Oh, dear nurse, I didn't know you were in the house," said Anna, rousing herself for a moment.
"I'm not living here, I'm living with my daughter. I came for the birthday, Anna Arkadyevna, darling!"
