The nurse suddenly burst into tears and started kissing her hand again.

Seryozha, his eyes shining and a smile on his face, was holding his mother by one hand and his nurse by the other, pattering on the rug with his fat little bare feet. The tenderness his beloved nurse was showing his mother had thrown him into an ecstasy.

"Mother! She often comes to see me, and when she does…" he was starting to say — then stopped, noticing that the nurse was whispering something to his mother, and that on his mother's face there was a look of fear and something like shame, which sat so strangely on her.
She went up to him.
"My sweet!" she said.

She couldn't bring herself to say _good-bye_, but the look on her face said it, and he understood. "Darling, darling Kootik!" — she used the name she had called him by when he was little — "you won't forget me? You.…" but she couldn't go on.

How often afterward she thought of the things she could have said. But now she didn't know how to say it, and could say nothing. Yet Seryozha understood everything she wanted to tell him. He understood that she was unhappy and that she loved him. He even understood what the nurse had whispered. He had caught the words "always at nine o'clock," and he knew that this was about his father, and that his father and mother couldn't meet. He understood all that — only one thing he couldn't understand: why was there a look of fear and shame on her face? She wasn't in the wrong, and yet she was afraid of him and ashamed of something. He would have liked to ask a question that would clear up that doubt, but he didn't dare; he could see that she was miserable, and he felt for her. Silently he pressed himself against her and whispered, "Don't go yet. He won't come yet."

The mother held him away from her to see what he was thinking, and what to say to him. In his frightened face she read not only that he was talking about his father, but that he was, in a sense, asking her what he ought to think about his father.
"Seryozha, my darling," she said, "love him. He's better and kinder than I am, and I've done him wrong. When you're grown up you'll judge it."

"There's no one better than you!" he cried in despair through his tears, and, gripping her by the shoulders, he started squeezing her against him with all his strength, his arms shaking with the effort.
"My sweet, my little one!" said Anna, and she cried as helplessly and childishly as he was crying.
At that moment the door opened. Vassily Lukitch came in.
From the other door came the sound of footsteps, and the nurse said in a frightened whisper, "He's coming," and handed Anna her hat.

Seryozha sank down on the bed and sobbed, hiding his face in his hands. Anna pulled his hands away, kissed his wet face one more time, and walked quickly to the door. Alexey Alexandrovitch came in, meeting her. Seeing her, he stopped short and bowed his head.

Even though she had just said he was better and kinder than she was, in the quick glance she shot at him, taking in every detail of his figure, feelings of revulsion and hatred toward him, and jealousy over her son, took hold of her. With a swift movement she dropped her veil and, picking up her pace, almost ran out of the room.
She didn't have time to undo it, and so carried back with her the parcel of toys she had picked out the day before, with such love and sorrow, in the toy shop.

title: Chapter 31
paragraphs: However much Anna had longed to see her son, however long she'd been thinking about it and preparing for it, she had had no idea that the meeting would affect her so deeply. Back in her empty rooms at the hotel, she couldn't for a long time grasp why she was even there. "Yes, it's all over, and I'm alone again," she said to herself, and without taking off her hat she sank into a low chair by the hearth. Fixing her eyes on a bronze clock on a table between the windows, she tried to think.
The French maid she'd brought from abroad came in to suggest she dress. Anna looked at her blankly and said, "Later." A footman offered her coffee. "Later," she said.

The Italian nurse, after taking the baby out in her best clothes, came in with her and brought her to Anna. The plump, well-fed little baby caught sight of her mother and, as she always did, held out her fat little hands. With a smile on her toothless mouth she began, like a fish flicking a float, bobbing her fingers up and down over the starched folds of her embroidered skirt, making them rustle. It was impossible not to smile, not to kiss the baby, not to hold out a finger for her to grab while she cooed and pranced; impossible not to offer her a lip that she sucked into her little mouth by way of a kiss. Anna did all of this — took the baby up, swung her about, kissed her fresh little cheek and bare little elbows — but the sight of this child only made it clearer than ever to her that what she felt for her could not be called love compared to what she felt for Seryozha. Everything about the baby was charming, but somehow none of it touched her deeply. On her first child — though the child of an unloved father — had been concentrated all the love that had never found an outlet. Her baby girl had been born under the most painful circumstances and had received not a hundredth of the care and attention that had gone into her firstborn. Besides, with the little girl everything was still in the future, while Seryozha was by now almost a person, and a person dearly loved. There was a struggle of thought and feeling inside him; he understood her, he loved her, he was judging her, she thought, remembering his words and his eyes. And she was forever cut off from him — not just physically but spiritually — and there was no way to set it right.

She handed the baby back to the nurse, dismissed them, and opened the locket that held a portrait of Seryozha at almost the same age as the little girl. She got up, took off her hat, and lifted from a small table an album of photographs of her son at different ages. She wanted to compare them and started taking the pictures out of the album. She got them all out except one — the latest and best photograph. In it he was in a white smock, sitting astride a chair, with frowning eyes and smiling lips. It was his best, most characteristic expression. With her small supple hands, her white, delicate fingers, which today moved with a peculiar tension, she tugged at the corner of the photograph, but it had snagged somewhere and she couldn't get it out. There was no paper-knife on the table, so she pulled out the photograph next to her son's — a picture of Vronsky taken in Rome in a round hat, with long hair — and used it to push out Seryozha's. "Oh, here he is!" she said, glancing at the portrait of Vronsky, and she suddenly remembered that he was the cause of her present misery. She hadn't once thought of him all morning. But now, coming all at once on that strong, noble face, so familiar and dear to her, she felt a sudden surge of love for him.

"But where is he? How can he leave me alone in this misery?" she thought all at once, with a feeling of reproach — forgetting that she herself had hidden everything to do with her son from him. She sent word asking him to come at once; with a pounding heart she waited for him, rehearsing the words in which she would tell him everything and the words of love with which he would comfort her. The messenger came back with the reply that he had a visitor, but that he would come immediately and was asking whether she would let him bring Prince Yashvin, who had just arrived in Petersburg. "He's not coming alone, and since dinner yesterday he hasn't seen me," she thought. "He's not coming so I can tell him everything — he's coming with Yashvin." And all at once a strange thought struck her: what if he had stopped loving her?

And as she went over the events of the past few days, it seemed to her she saw confirmation of that terrible idea everywhere. The fact that he hadn't dined at home yesterday, the fact that he had insisted on their taking separate suites of rooms in Petersburg, and the fact that even now he wasn't coming to her alone, as though he were trying to avoid being face to face with her.

"But he ought to say so. I have to know that it's so. If I knew it, then I'd know what to do," she said to herself, completely unable to picture what her life would look like if she were certain he no longer loved her. She thought he had stopped loving her, she felt close to despair, and as a result she felt unusually alert. She rang for her maid and went into her dressing room. As she dressed, she took more care over her appearance than she had all those days — as if, supposing he had cooled toward her, he might fall in love with her again because she had dressed and arranged her hair in the way that suited her best.

She heard the bell ring before she was ready. When she came into the drawing room it wasn't he but Yashvin she saw. Vronsky was looking at the photographs of her son, which she had left out on the table, and he was in no hurry to turn around to her.

"We've met already," she said, putting her small hand into Yashvin's huge one — Yashvin, whose bashfulness was so oddly at odds with his enormous frame and coarse face. "We met last year at the races. Give those to me," she said, snatching the photographs of her son from Vronsky with a swift movement and shooting him a meaningful, flashing-eyed glance. "Were the races good this year? Instead of them I saw the races in the Corso in Rome. But you don't care for life abroad," she added with a friendly smile. "I know you, and I know all your tastes, even though I've seen so little of you."
"I'm awfully sorry for that, since most of my tastes are bad," said Yashvin, gnawing at his left mustache.

After they had talked a little while, and after Yashvin noticed that Vronsky glanced at the clock, he asked her whether she would be staying in Petersburg much longer, and unfolded his huge frame to reach for his cap.
"Not long, I think," she said hesitantly, glancing at Vronsky.
"So we shan't meet again, then?"

"Come and dine with me," Anna said firmly, seeming angry with herself for her own awkwardness, but flushing as she always did when she had to define her position in front of someone new. "The dinner here is nothing special, but at least you'll see him. There's no one of his old regiment friends Alexey is as fond of as he is of you."
"Delighted," said Yashvin with a smile, and from that smile Vronsky could tell he liked Anna very much.
Yashvin said good-bye and went out. Vronsky stayed behind.
"Are you going too?" she said to him.
"I'm late already," he answered. "Go on ahead! I'll catch you up in a minute," he called to Yashvin.
She took him by the hand and, without taking her eyes off him, looked at him while she searched for words that would keep him.
"Wait a minute, there's something I want to say to you," and, taking his broad hand, she pressed it against her neck. "Oh — was it right of me to invite him to dinner?"
"You did absolutely the right thing," he said with a serene smile that showed his even teeth, and he kissed her hand.
"Alexey, you haven't changed toward me?" she said, gripping his hand in both of hers. "Alexey, I'm miserable here. When are we leaving?"
"Soon, soon. You wouldn't believe how unpleasant this way of life is for me too," he said, and pulled his hand away.
"Well, go, go!" she said in an offended tone, and walked off quickly from him.
